This redemption is not ideal for beginners — it scores 2/5 on beginner-friendliness, and honestly, that's accurate. The booking path involves navigating partner award searches, understanding the difference between booking programs (Alaska vs. JAL Mileage Bank) and why it matters for surcharges, and potentially calling airlines rather than booking online. If you're on your first or second travel rewards card and still building your foundational understanding, this is one to put on a future list while you sharpen your skills.

For the FI-focused traveler who has been in the travel rewards ecosystem for a year or more, this is a landmark redemption. The CPP ceiling of 16.7 cents per point represents one of the highest-value uses of any points in a North American loyalty portfolio. If you believe in maximizing every dollar you earn and every point you accumulate — and the ChooseFI community does — this is the kind of redemption that justifies the entire system.

According to recent reports, this redemption is rated **moderate difficulty**, and that rating is honest. It's not the most complex thing in the travel rewards world, but it has enough moving parts that going in without preparation can lead to frustration or costly mistakes. **What specifically makes it moderate:** First, the **earning path is not plug-and-play**. Unlike Chase Ultimate Rewards or Amex Membership Rewards, which transfer to dozens of partners instantly, Alaska miles and American miles are earned primarily through co-branded credit cards and flying. There's no one magic transferable currency that flows directly into these programs at full value. Second, **the booking process often requires a phone call**. Online partner award booking through Alaska and American works inconsistently. Many experienced travelers report that calling the airline's award desk surfaces availability that the website doesn't show — which is a normal part of the process but adds friction. Third, **fuel surcharge awareness matters**. Understanding *why* you book through Alaska or American instead of JAL Mileage Bank directly is a non-obvious nuance that could cost you real money if you don't get it right. **Three tips to overcome the challenge:** 1. **Use BA.com as your availability scouting tool** — it gives you a clean, visual look at JAL award space without committing any miles. 2. **Call Alaska or American directly** when online searches fail. Agents are well-versed in partner award booking and can often find and hold space while you confirm your miles balance. 3. **Build your miles balance before you start searching.** Having 70,000+ miles in hand (a small buffer above 60,000) before you begin reduces stress and gives you flexibility on dates. If you've already completed one or two simpler travel rewards bookings and understand the basics of award searches, this is well within reach. The effort is real — and the payoff is a flat bed over the Pacific.

According to recent reports, go to ba.com (British Airways Executive Club) and search for your route in business class. Because BA is a oneworld partner, their search tool reveals JAL award space. Search across multiple dates to find availability. Any space you see here is almost certainly bookable through Alaska or American as well.

According to recent reports, both charge 60,000 miles one-way with no fuel surcharges. Alaska miles can be earned through the Alaska Airlines Visa card or transferred from Marriott Bonvoy® (3:1). AAdvantage miles can be earned through Citi cards or transferred from various hotel programs. Choose based on which miles you have or can earn most efficiently.

Only transfer points after confirming award availability on ba.com. For Alaska, earn through card spending or Marriott transfers. For AAdvantage, earn through Citi cards. Never transfer before confirming space — transfers are generally irreversible.

Call Alaska Mileage Plan or book on aa.com to ticket the JAL-operated flight. For Alaska, phone booking is required for partner awards. For AA, search on aa.com and book online if the JAL space appears. Confirm your JAL seat assignment on jal.com after ticketing.

JAL Mileage Bank imposes fuel surcharges on its own award tickets, often adding $100 to $500 per ticket on transpacific routes. Alaska Mileage Strategy and American AAdvantage book the exact same JAL-operated flights at the same 60,000-mile price but with zero fuel surcharges. You fly the same plane, same seat, same service — but pay significantly less out of pocket.

JAL opens its award calendar approximately 360 days in advance. For peak seasons like cherry blossom season (late March to early April) and Golden Week (late April to early May), you should begin searching the day the window opens. Off-peak dates are generally easier to find with 3 to 6 months of lead time.

In a recent development, not directly, but you can use Chase points indirectly. Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards to British Airways Avios and book JAL through BA's oneworld partnership. However, BA charges fuel surcharges on partner awards, so this path is less favorable than Alaska or AA. The cleanest Chase path is to earn Alaska or AA miles through other means.

Industry observers note that JAL Sky Suite business class features angled lie-flat or fully lie-flat seats depending on the aircraft, with a privacy shell, excellent Japanese cuisine, attentive service, and premium amenity kits. The service quality is consistently praised as among the best in the industry. On 777-300ER and 787 aircraft, the product competes with top-tier offerings from Singapore Airlines and Cathay Pacific.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

It has been revealed that JAL business class via Alaska Mileage Plan or American AAdvantage is the definitive sweet spot for anyone targeting Japan. At 60,000 miles one-way with zero fuel surcharges, you are booking a $5,000 to $10,000 cash experience for a fraction of the cost through a partner program pricing arbitrage. The key is searching ba.com for availability before transferring a single point, booking 360 days out for peak cherry blossom or Golden Week dates, and choosing between Alaska and AA based on which miles you can earn most efficiently. JAL's business class product — lie-flat seats, exceptional cuisine, and Japanese hospitality — delivers an experience that justifies the points spend and then some. This is the redemption that puts Japan within reach for every FI-minded traveler.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that get ready for a medical emergency while you’re healthy.
  • A heart attack or bad car crash can run up hospital bills while you’re too sick to speak for yourself.
  • In a recent development, most health looks cap your share of those bills at an out-of-pocket maximum, the most you pay in a blueprint year for covered in-network care.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that get ready for a medical emergency while you’re healthy. Keep savings equal to your health proposal’s out-of-pocket maximum, and make sure disability coverage would replace part of your paycheck. Then sign a health care proxy and a HIPAA release so someone you trust can talk to your doctors and decide for you.

A heart attack or bad car crash can run up hospital bills while you’re too sick to speak for yourself.

In a recent development, most health looks cap your share of those bills at an out-of-pocket maximum, the most you pay in a blueprint year for covered in-network care. It’s on page one of your plan’s Summary of Benefits and Coverage, called the out-of-pocket limit. Save that much.

Say a married couple’s family initiative caps their share at $9,000 a year. They keep $9,000 in a health savings account, and each has signed a health care proxy naming the other to make medical decisions. When one has a heart attack, the account pays their share, and the proxy settles who decides. Without one, state law would usually pick the spouse, but a relative could contest that in court.

Industry observers note that keep that money in a health savings account if your plan qualifies, since the balance carries over and withdrawals for qualified medical bills are tax-free. If not, build it into your emergency fund with automatic deposits each payday. If illness keeps you out of work for months, disability insurance through your job or your own policy replaces part of your pay.

Sources indicate that sign your own proxy, also called a health care power of attorney, and a living will, which tells doctors what treatment you’d want if you can’t decide for yourself. One form, an advance directive, usually covers both. Add a HIPAA release, which names who can get your medical information, since some providers want permission in writing. Keep copies, with a list of your medications and doctors, where family can find them.

In a recent development, after a serious diagnosis, ask your insurer whether it offers a case manager, usually a nurse or social worker, to help coordinate your care. Nonprofit hospitals must have a written financial assistance policy, which can mean free or discounted care, so ask for the application before the first bill.

Industry observers note that start with the forms, since they cost little or nothing. CaringInfo posts every state’s advance directive form free, and you don’t need a lawyer. Give copies to the person you name and your doctor.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

Recent findings suggest that having more than one type of debt is common, and that’s especially true once you graduate from college and start your first “real job.” You may have credit card debt, an auto loan, and a mortgage payment to make once you buy your first home. It’s also common to have other random debts to cover, including student loans.

Recent findings suggest that if you’re like many who took out loans during college, you will likely be paying them off after you graduate. In fact, 82% of students who borrowed loans expect to be making payments post-graduation, according to a recent College Ave Student Loans survey.

That said, you’ll want to make sure you’re balancing debt repayment with your savings goals along the way.

You’ll also want to make sure you’re paying down debts in the optimal order, or in a way that will help you save the most money on interest as possible while aligning with your goals. Which debts should you pay off first? Here’s a rundown of how to get the best results:.

According to recent reports, no matter which types of debt you have, credit card debt should be your first priority. Why? Because credit card debt is likely the most expensive debt you have by far.

Federal Reserve data shows the average credit card interest rate on accounts assessed interest came in at around 22% as of May 2023, yet your credit card could easily be charging higher rates than the average.

Sources indicate that to save as much money as possible, you should strive to pay as much as you can toward high-interest credit card bills each month. You can also pay down credit card debt faster with the help of a debt consolidation loan or a 0% APR balance transfer credit card.

Recent findings suggest that other unsecured debts like personal loan debt should come next in the debt payoff pecking order. After all, unsecured debts tend to have higher interest rates than secured debts like auto loans. In fact, the Federal Reserve also reported that the average interest rate on a 24-month personal loan came in at 11.48% as of May 2023, compared to the average rate of 7.81% on a 60-month auto loan.

Ideally, you’ll start paying more toward personal loan debt and other unsecured debts after all credit card debt is entirely paid off, although you should make at least the minimum payment on all your bills throughout the entire process.

According to recent reports, the next debt you’ll want to tackle is your student loans. I suggest focusing on these loans after other unsecured debts, since federal student loans (and many private student loans) come with low fixed interest rates and monthly payments that will not change over time. If you have federal student loans, you may even want to look into income-driven repayment intends.

According to recent reports, if you’re hoping to pay down student loans faster or just want to save money on interest, you can also consider refinancing your student loans to get a shorter repayment timeline, a lower monthly payment, or both. Just remember that refinancing federal student loans can mean losing access to income-driven repayment prepares and federal protections like deferment and forbearance.

In a recent development, once you have paid off or substantially paid down all your other debts, you can focus your efforts on secured debts you have like mortgage loans and auto loans. These debts should be dealt with last since they are secured with collateral and tend to offer lower interest rates as a result. For example, you can consider paying more than the minimum on your mortgage, a car loan, or both until they’re paid off completely.

Then again, you may want to pay off debts with extremely low interest rates as slowly as possible to free up more cash flow for living expenses and investments. If you took out a mortgage in January of 2021 when the average interest rate on a 30-year, fixed rate home loan was as low as 2.65%, for example, it makes sense to make the minimum payment on that debt and invest your extra cash instead.

Recent findings suggest that it’s vital to make sure you balance debt repayment with other financial considerations. After all, focusing too much on debt repayment early in life can leave you behind when it comes to investing for retirement or saving up for a first home.

While you’ll want to eliminate credit card debt and other high-interest debts as quickly as you can, even if you have to stop saving and investing for a while, you can pay down student loan debt and secured debts at a slower pace while saving and investing for the future along the way.

It has been revealed that finally, make sure you have adequate emergency savings throughout your entire debt payoff journey, or that you begin saving for emergencies as soon as you can. Without a fully funded emergency fund, you can end up relying on credit cards and other loans to get by and ruin your debt payoff progress in the process.

Sources indicate that how much should you save? While most experts recommend having an emergency fund that can cover three to six months of expenses, it’s okay to start small if you have to.

Sources indicate that having more than one type of debt is how it works for most people, especially when you’re young and in the early stages of your career. When it comes to paying it off, however, you’ll want to make sure you have a concrete plan that can help you reduce interest charges and get where you want to be.

According to recent reports, focusing on credit card debt and other unsecured debts first always makes sense, since these debts aren’t secured by an asset and tend to charge much higher interest rates. You can focus on student loans next, followed by other secured debts you have like a home loan or car loan.

In the meantime, make sure you have an adequate emergency fund and invest in it for retirement. After all, debt won’t last forever if you’re serious about repayment, and saving and investing early can help you benefit from compound interest and avoid using credit cards for surprise expenses. Creating a budget to track these factors is your best bet.

If you need help creating one, or simply don’t know where to start, use this budget worksheet as your guide – you’ll reach financial freedom in no time.

According to recent reports, A couple of years ago, Mr. Money Mustache lost some credibility among the faithful when he wrote this blog post about actually trying to spend a bit more money, while buying a Tesla as the first step in that program.

I thought to myself at the time,.

“I’m such an enlightened middle-aged Badass, adjusting habits and realigning myself at the snap of my fingers. Onward to the next forty eight years of the Good Life!”.

Recent findings suggest that so, two years passed with an even greater feeling of abundance. I had a marvelous time traveling everywhere and spending money like I thought a proper wealthy person would do.

I dined out in stylish restaurants, booked hotels based on their niceness rather than their cheapness, paid extra to sit in the “reduced torture” seats of the airplanes, and gave zero fucks about paying double for groceries if I happened to be in a Whole Foods rather than my usual Sam’s Club and Costco (and yes I treat myself to memberships at both warehouse stores!).

Industry observers note that among the highlights, my son and I have worked our way though a nice selection of late night EDM concerts and three Meowwolf art venues including a Christmas Day road trip from our winter home in Tempe Arizona to Las Vegas last year. And having spent much of the year as a single man, I had a wide open schedule to just meet up with friends, explore upcoming places and meet new people as opportunities came up. It felt like a year of adventurous transition, which means it felt like much more than twelve months.

In a recent development, with all this flashy spending, I was sure my budget must have crept back into full American Consumer territory. But I was having too much fun to bother adding it all up to check.

Until recently, when I was doing another round of informal coaching for a friend and we both decided to tally our spending for the past year to compare notes.

When I finally finished sorting all of those transactions into a spreadsheet and hit the “sum” button, the results surprised me.

According to recent reports, while my overall spending had indeed increased (especially in travel-related categories), the massive-picture effect was still pretty minimal. Depending on how I account for things like the car and my business expenses, my spending went from $20,000 to about $30,000 (plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house.).

This level could still be sustained by a $1 million investment nest egg. Since my investments are quite a bit higher than that (especially after these recent years of crazy economic growth and the never-ending stock market rally), I’m still way under budget.

Although I still “failed” to really increase my spending to the MMM-recommended levels for old wealthy people, this still makes me happy, because I have genuinely had more fun with the abundance mindset, and I can keep trying more life experiments in the coming years.

Sources indicate that as we covered in the 2019 article on the idea of an Optimization Council, it’s always a good idea to compare our spending, tips and tricks on how to get the most out of life. Almost twenty years into early retirement, this is where I have landed so far, although I’m always learning and open to feedback.

Anyway, let’s cut the wistful commentary and get into the budget.

In summary: Wow, how interesting! When we compare this to my 2019 post on that year’s spending, it’s only a bit higher even after all the inflation we have seen in recent years. I spent more on travel and fun, but less on home renovation – partly because I was away so much I didn’t have as much time to work on my house. The health insurance is a new cost too since I was self-insured back then.

My budget is notably missing the biggest expense for most people, which is housing costs. This is because I paid off my house long ago, and I also love working on and taking care of my own home, which means there are no bills for lawn mowing, plumbers, tree pruning or handyman services.

According to recent reports, this strategy is not for everyone, and it’s not even the optimum financial one for me – I would have been better off taking out the biggest mortgage I could get at 3% back in the sweet borrowing times of 2021, and putting all that principal to work in stock index funds where it would have almost doubled since then. But I still get a great peace of mind from just having no mortgage payment, and there’s really no better way to use your money than to buy such good feelings. Also, I get a secondary benefit of not having to buy house insurance, which saves me another $2000 per year, boosting my effective return on that payoff.

First of all, the biggest money saving factor of good health and good luck has continued, meaning I’ve still had no actual medical expenses. But I still do maintain two layers of health care support which together feel very much like the ultimate version of health insurance: a membership with a top of the line Direct Primary Care (DPC) medical clinic ($107 per month) plus a high-deductible initiative ($201) with a health sharing organization called Sedera.

The combined cost of $308 per month is less than the cheapest Bronze blueprint in the field of standard health insurance, yet I get personalized support with zero deductible for almost all typical medical needs, plus some protection from larger medical bills if my good luck runs out.

It has been revealed that but as a disclaimer, I’m not an expert on medical needs and health insurance because I’ve had so little experience with the system. And the highest priority in my life is arranging my days for maximum health to give me the best chance of keeping it this way.

When it comes down to it, money is a tool for survival and if we’re lucky, self actualization. So I’m always asking myself if there’s anything I can change or improve to make the most of this good fortune.

I also try to keep in mind an interesting principle of happiness, which notes that,.

Fixing your persistent problems is more effective than just doubling down on things that are already good in your life.

In a recent development, for me, there are already a lot of good things which don’t need improving. My family, friends, relationships, health, food and daily activities are pretty much as good as I could imagine.

The only annoyance I can think of is physical chaos: I have a lot of space-intensive hobbies like construction and music, and I currently live in a pretty small house which is basically maxed out. I could really use a doubling of my workshop space from the current 2-car, 440 square foot garage to maybe a thousand or so.

Sources indicate that but I also love where I live and wouldn’t want to give up my views, neighbors or current place. So I’ll keep optimizing what I’ve got unless some perfect opportunity comes up for a bigger place right on my block.

In the longer run, a mountain compound with its own cliffs and stream are also on my “maybe” list. But once again, my days and life are already overbooked with joyful things. My existing house and our HQ Coworking space already have long to-do lists. Would I actually be happier if I added another place to my portfolio? So I keep this idea on the shelf until I’m willing to trade it for another existing commitment – like selling my house or the coworking space.

Sources indicate that but for now, I’m just extremely excited to blaze into 2025 with loads abundance and piles of challenging stuff on my to-do list. And I wish you the same!

What Are Target Date Funds?

📅 27 May 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1218 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Wellkeptwallet

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.
  • Sources indicate that A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment.
  • Industry observers note that the fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In this article, we will break down what target date funds are, how they work, what they cost, and why a low-cost index fund strategy may serve most investors better in the long run.

Sources indicate that A target-date fund is a type of mutual fund designed to serve as a single, all-in-one retirement investment. You pick the fund that most closely matches the year you proposal to retire, and the fund handles everything else. If you plan to retire around 2050, for example, you would choose a fund labeled something like “2050 Retirement Fund” or “Target Date 2050.”.

Industry observers note that the fund holds a mix of stocks and bonds, and that mix automatically shifts over time as your target date gets closer. Early on, the fund is weighted heavily toward growth stocks. As retirement approaches, the portfolio gradually shifts toward bonds and more conservative holdings to reduce risk.

The appeal is obvious. You make one decision, contribute regularly, and the fund adjusts itself. For people who want to set it and forget it, that sounds like a dream. But there is more to the story.

Target date funds are known as “fund of funds.” Rather than holding individual stocks or bonds directly, they hold a collection of other mutual funds, typically a mix of domestic stock, international stock, and bond funds.

The fund manager adjusts the allocation over time according to a schedule called a glide path. When you are decades away from retirement, the fund might hold 90% stocks and 10% bonds. As you get closer to your target year, that ratio shifts until the fund is much more conservative, sometimes holding more bonds than stocks by the time you retire.

In a recent development, the glide path is simply the schedule that determines how the fund’s asset allocation changes over time. Think of it as the fund’s long-term plan for gradually reducing risk.

Different fund providers use different glide paths, and this matters more than most people realize. Some funds are more aggressive early on and pull back dramatically as retirement nears. Others maintain a higher stock allocation even into and through retirement, which some financial planners argue is actually smarter given how long retirement can last.

Industry observers note that the important thing to understand is that the glide path is not customized for you. It is a one-size-fits-all formula based on your expected retirement year, nothing more. Your actual risk tolerance, health, spending prepares, and other income sources are not factored in at all.

According to recent reports, the biggest selling point is that target date funds require almost no ongoing attention. You pick one fund, contribute regularly, and walk away. For someone who has no interest in managing their investments, that convenience is genuinely valuable.

Because target date funds hold a mix of stock and bond funds, you get broad diversification across asset classes in a single investment. You are not putting all your money into a single sector or company.

It has been revealed that over time, a portfolio can drift away from its intended allocation as different assets grow at different rates. Target date funds handle this automatically, which is one less thing you have to manage yourself.

Target date funds are not without their drawbacks, and for many investors, those drawbacks are significant enough to look for a better option.

Because target date funds are funds of funds, they often carry two layers of fees: the expense ratio of the target date fund itself and the underlying expense ratios of the funds it holds. Even a seemingly small difference in fees can cost you tens of thousands of dollars over a long investing career. Low-cost index funds, by comparison, often charge a fraction of what target date funds do.

According to recent reports, the glide path in a target-date fund is designed for the average investor retiring in a given year. But your situation is not average. You might have a pension, a working spouse, rental income, or a much higher risk tolerance than the fund assumes. None of that is reflected in how the fund manages your money.

When you hand everything over to a target date fund, you give up control over your allocation. If the fund has a heavy position in international stocks or bonds that you would rather avoid, there is not much you can do about it while staying in the fund.

Variable quality across providers.

Not all target date funds are created equal. The same target year fund from two different providers can have very different allocations, fee structures, and underlying holdings. Without digging into the details, it is easy to end up in a fund that does not match your actual needs.

This is where the comparison gets important. A target date fund is actively managed in the sense that a team of people decides how to allocate and rebalance it over time. An index fund, on the other hand, simply tracks a market index like the S&P 500. There is no active management involved, which is exactly why the fees are so much lower.

Decades of research consistently show that most actively managed funds underperform their benchmark index after fees. Target date funds are not immune to this problem. When you account for layered costs, many target-date funds trail what you would earn by simply holding a low-cost index fund over the same period.

According to recent reports, A simple alternative that many investors use is called a three-fund portfolio: a U.S. total market index fund, an international index fund, and a bond index fund. You set your own allocation based on your age and risk tolerance, rebalance once a year, and pay minimal fees. It takes about 30 minutes a year to manage.

It has been revealed that this approach gives you the same diversification as a target-date fund, with far more control and significantly lower costs. And as a general rule, the more of your return you keep rather than paying in fees, the better off you will be over time.

Target date funds are not the right choice for every investor, but there are situations where they make sense.

In a recent development, even in these cases, it is worth checking the expense ratio. If your strategy offers a target-date fund with an expense ratio above 0.50%, consider whether there are lower-cost index fund options within the same plan.

Target date funds solve a real problem: they make it easy for people who do not want to think about investing to still participate in the market. That convenience has real value.

It has been revealed that but for investors who are willing to learn even a little bit about how to manage their own allocation, a portfolio of low-cost index funds will almost always be the better long-term choice. The fees are lower, the control is greater, and the returns tend to be better over time.

If you are presently in a target date fund, that is not necessarily a problem. But it is worth understanding what you are paying and whether a simpler, lower-cost approach might serve you better. Investing at least 10% of your gross income is the priority. Where exactly that money goes is the next question worth asking.

Sources indicate that the cheapest flight usually goes to the traveler who can shift dates or airports. Search a calendar of fares instead of fixed dates, include every airport near you, and set a price alert so you can book when the fare dips. Compare fares only after adding the bags and seat you’ll pay for.

Industry observers note that changing only your travel days can cut the fare. Google’s analysis of five years of its flight data found that leaving on a Monday and returning on a Tuesday or Wednesday costs about 14% less than flying on the weekend.

Industry observers note that on Google Flights, open the date grid or price graph to see which travel dates around your trip have the lowest fares. Add every airport within an easy drive to the search, since a smaller airport nearby can be cheaper than your closest one. Also compare the round-trip fare with two one-way tickets on different airlines.

Industry observers note that say a family of four moves its departure from Saturday to Tuesday and flies from a smaller airport 40 minutes away, and each round-trip ticket costs $90 less. That’s $360 saved, minus gas for the longer drive.

Then turn on price tracking for the route, so Google emails you when the price changes significantly. Google’s analysis found domestic fares low from 22 to 57 days before departure and cheapest around 39 days out. International fares were low from 50 to 133 days out. For Thanksgiving or Christmas, book holiday flights in October instead of waiting for a sale.

It has been revealed that before you compare a basic economy or budget airline fare with a regular one, add the extras you’ll pay for. Basic economy, an airline’s most restricted ticket, usually limits bags and comes without a seat assignment. Google Flights’ bags filter adds checked or carry-on bag fees to the prices it highlights. Add the cost of choosing a seat for each traveler who needs one.

Book the lowest total on the airline’s own site. The Transportation Department’s 24-hour rule covers tickets bought at least seven days before departure. Under it, the airline must either give a full refund on a ticket canceled within 24 hours or hold the fare for 24 hours without payment. Tickets bought through travel booking sites and agents aren’t covered.

Run your next fare search on Google Flights.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that picture an office worker who trades her desk for a mail route.
  • Sources indicate that the difference shows up in calories.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Plenty of jobs pay you to walk, lift, and climb instead of sitting, and some pay well above the typical U.S. wage. Before you switch, compare each job’s pay and training with what it asks of your body, since the active jobs you can start fastest tend to pay the least.

Recent findings suggest that picture an office worker who trades her desk for a mail route. She now spends most of her shift on her feet, and the exercise she used to pay a gym for comes with the job.

Sources indicate that the difference shows up in calories. The Compendium of Physical Activities, a research list rating how much energy activities take, scores each one against sitting quietly, which burns about 1 calorie an hour for every 2.2 pounds you weigh. For a 160-pound person, that puts an hour of office work at about 110 calories, delivering mail on foot at about 170, general yard work at about 290, and firefighting at about 580.

Carriers on walking routes cover about 4 to 12 miles a day and spend up to about six hours on foot, the National Association of Letter Carriers says. Over those six hours, a 160-pound carrier burns roughly 350 more calories than she would at a desk. The 15 jobs below run from that kind of steady walking to heavy lifting, and their pay ranges just as widely.

Pay below is each job’s May 2025 median from the Occupational Outlook Handbook of the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS), meaning half of workers in the job earn more and half less. For comparison, the median for all U.S. workers was $50,980.

The quickest jobs to start mostly pay the least. Animal care, grounds work, material moving, construction labor, and fitness training take little or no schooling, and all five pay under the $50,980 national median. Mail carriers are the exception. The other better-paid jobs here typically start with a training program, a degree, or an apprenticeship.

In a recent development, physical work also brings more injuries than a desk job. BLS counts construction laborers, material movers, and flight attendants among the occupations with the highest injury and illness rates, and nurses and therapist assistants who lift patients are prone to back injuries.

The strain adds up with age. A University of Michigan Retirement and Disability Research Center study found that workers in more physically demanding jobs are more likely to be retired at any given age. The effect highlighted up almost entirely in men and was larger among those without a college degree. That makes saving early matter more in a heavy job, since your working years may be fewer.

To earn while you train, start with the trades. Electricians and elevator installers learn through apprenticeships that pay for their hours on the job, and carpenters can train the same way. The Labor Department’s Apprenticeship Finder lets you search openings by career and location.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that inflation, the steady rise in prices, shrinks what each dollar you hold in cash can buy, even at the modest pace the Federal Reserve aims for. Keep your emergency fund and money you’ll spend within five years in savings, and invest the rest, since stocks have grown faster than prices over long periods.

In a recent development, the Federal Reserve aims for inflation of 2% a year over the long run, and even that pace doubles prices in about 35 years, so a dollar kept in cash buys half as much. In the 12 months through June 2022, prices rose 9.1%, the biggest jump in 40 years, the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) reported.

According to recent reports, prices climb when spending outruns what businesses can supply, or when costs like energy and wages rise and get passed on to shoppers. Expectations push them up too, since people who expect higher prices ask for bigger raises and buy sooner. Savers holding cash and retirees on a pension that never rises lose ground. Borrowers with fixed-rate loans gain, since they repay in dollars that buy less, and workers whose raises keep pace hold their own.

Sources indicate that prices rose about 92% from January 2000 to December 2025, by the government’s Consumer Price Index. By the end, $10,000 left in a checking account that paid no interest bought only what about $5,200 bought in 2000, as the BLS’s CPI Inflation Calculator demonstrates. Interest shrinks that loss, but only a rate above inflation, a positive real interest rate, adds buying power. So sort your money by when you’ll spend it.

Keep your emergency fund and money you’ll need within five years in a high-yield savings account, where it earns interest and can’t drop with stock prices. Invest the rest in low-cost index funds, which own hundreds or thousands of stocks at once, through your 401(k), an individual retirement account (IRA), or a brokerage account.

With dividends reinvested and before fees and taxes, $10,000 invested in the S&P 500, an index of 500 large U.S. companies, grew to about $73,900 over those years, by our math from NYU professor Aswath Damodaran’s return data. That $73,900 bought what about $38,500 bought in 2000, despite a 37% loss in 2008, which is why only money you can leave alone for years belongs in stocks.

Total your emergency fund and the next five years of planned spending, keep that much in savings, and invest every dollar beyond it.

The mechanism behind Flying Blue Promo Rewards is elegantly simple once you understand it, and it separates this program from virtually every other airline loyalty play in your toolkit.

Flying Blue Has a Dynamic Award Chart — With a Monthly Override.

Recent findings suggest that flying Blue moved to dynamic pricing, which typically means the program is less predictable and often less valuable than the old fixed-chart days. But here's where it gets interesting: Promo Rewards operate as a fixed-price overlay on top of that dynamic system. On the 1st of each month (or within the first few days), Flying Blue publishes a curated list of routes — often 20 to 40 city pairs — with fixed, deeply discounted mile prices. Business class seats on transatlantic routes regularly appear at 40,000 to 50,000 miles one-way. These are not dynamic prices that will creep up as demand increases. They're locked promotional rates on specific routes.

This means the program essentially gives you two separate games to play: the chaotic dynamic pricing game (usually skip it), and the monthly Promo Rewards game (always pay attention).

It has been revealed that for a family trip of three nights or more, compare a hotel suite, extended-stay room, or rental with a kitchen to a standard room. Add up the kitchen’s extra cost for the whole stay, any cleaning fee included, and book the one with the kitchen if cooking breakfast and a few dinners would save your family more than that.

According to recent reports, that extra cost highlights up in the nightly rate. The savings show up at every meal your family doesn’t buy at a restaurant.

Say a room with a kitchen costs your family of four $30 a night more than one without. Breakfast out costs $50 and dinner $100, against $15 and $30 for the same meals from a grocery store. Cooking breakfast saves $35 a day, which covers the $30 on its own.

It has been revealed that over five nights, cooking every breakfast and two dinners saves $315, or $165 after the kitchen’s extra $150. On a stay of a night or two, the kitchen often doesn’t pay off, because some costs come once per stay, such as the coffee, oil, and spices from your first grocery run. A rental’s cleaning fee is one of them. A $100 fee adds $50 a night to a two-night stay, more than the $35 a day you save by cooking breakfast, but only $20 a night to a five-night one.

It has been revealed that extended-stay chains put a kitchen in every room. Extended Stay America’s suites all have full kitchens, and the chain discounts longer stays. Candlewood Suites’ studios and suites come with full kitchens too. Some extended-stay chains also serve a free breakfast, so there the kitchen saves you money only on the other meals you cook. Check for a stovetop, since some kitchenettes have only a microwave.

On Airbnb or Vrbo, compare a rental’s total price for your dates with a hotel’s. Under the Federal Trade Commission’s fee rule, that total must include the cleaning fee, as a hotel’s must include any resort fee, though taxes can be added before you pay.

Industry observers note that shop on day one for breakfasts and two or three dinners that share ingredients, such as taco meat one night and burrito bowls the next. Initiative a dinner out every day or two so nobody spends the trip at the stove.

If cooking breakfast saves your family more than the kitchen’s extra cost per night, with any cleaning fee divided across your nights, the kitchen pays for itself before you cook a single dinner.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

And by lately, I mean the past several years or more.

The value of the S&P 500 index of stocks, where most of us hopefully have a good chunk of our retirement savings stashed into index funds, is up about fifty seven percent in just the past two years. And it has more than doubled in the past five.

This means that on a net worth basis, if you felt like you were only halfway to retirement as recently as the Covid Era, you may have suddenly blown right past the finish line. And some of us who were already retired long before that, may find ourselves eyeing up expensive properties or engaging in other money-burning-a-hole-in-our-pocket behaviors.

Is this real? Or is it all a bubble or some other sort of financial illusion?

As one reader recently asked me in an email:.

Sources indicate that “The market seems to be in a huge bubble right now due to all sorts of hype around Artificial Intelligence. Does this make it more vulnerable to a huge crash in the future, and will it affect my retirement?”.

Recent findings suggest that to answer this question, let’s take a closer look at our current somewhat unprecedented financial world and stock market. And to understand that properly, it helps to go back to the roots of what a stock is:.

A stock is a magical business arrangement which is really just a much more convenient version of a rental house.

Industry observers note that when you own a rental house, you are entitled to collect rent. After you cover all the expenses related to the house, you get to keep the rest, and this amount is your profit.

If the average sale price of rental houses in your area goes up but the tenant keeps paying you the same amount forever, it may look good on paper but it doesn’t really mean anything unless you sell the house. And then you’d just have to turn around and pay that same higher amount for a different rental house.

Recent findings suggest that your paycheck remains unchanged unless you can make your little house rental business more profitable. So you might squeeze in a basement apartment, do some renovations, streamline expenses, or do other things to increase your net earnings.

When you eventually sell that house to another investor, the price they are willing to pay should be based on that future stream of income.

For example, if the house brings in $2000 per month ($24,000 each year) and the sale price is $240,000, the next investor is buying a business with a price-to-earnings ratio of 10, because 240k/24k=10.

But if you manage to convince someone to hand over $480,000 for that same house, you’ve sold at a P/E of 20. This is a much better deal for you as the seller, but quite obviously a less rosy future for the investor buying it.

Sources indicate that now back to the stock market. If you put $100,000 in the market in 2019 and reinvested the dividends, today you’d already have an astonishing $256,960 (a 157% gain on your original investment).

But in that same time period, your share of manufacturer earnings from that $100,000 basket of stocks has only gone from $5290 to $7540 (a measly 42% gain) – information you can get from handy analysis sites like multpl.com.

In other words, the Price-to-earnings ratio has risen from about 20 back then, to about 30 today.

It has been revealed that so as stock investors here in 2025, we’re just like rental house investors finding that house prices have more than doubled while rents are only up by a bit. Which makes the landlord business a lot less profitable, and we should expect exactly the same thing as stock investor: lower future profits as a percentage of our portfolio value.

It has been revealed that that doesn’t mean it’s unprofitable to own either one of these things – stocks or rental houses. But it does mean that we should expect our future income from buying them at today’s higher price-to-earnings ratio should be lower than if we could get them on sale. It’s just basic math.

Sources indicate that but Wait! What if the Earnings are Rising?

In a recent development, let’s say you’re considering a rental house which is a bit overpriced based on today’s rent, but you happen to know that a big Apple campus is about to get built right nearby. At that point, you expect that rent will start climbing rapidly for many years to come. In this situation, you should be willing to pay more for those future earnings when you buy the house.

This is exactly why the price of an individual company’s stock will tend to rise when some good news comes out about the company. During the Covid era, people started buying more Peloton bikes so they could exercise at home, and investors (foolishly) believed this would be a permanent trend. So Peloton stock went way up. Later, reality sunk in that this was just a fad and Peloton sales returned back to normal levels, and so did the stock.

Sources indicate that but what does it mean when the entire market goes up to much higher levels? Does it mean our entire economy is expected to grow much more promptly?

In the case of the current stock market euphoria, not exactly. Because if you dig into the share prices of the 500 big companies that make up our famous S&P 500 index, it turns out that almost all the recent growth – about three quarters of it – came from just the seven biggest companies, known as the Magnificent Seven: Apple, Nvidia, Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Facebook, and sometimes Tesla.

It has been revealed that these are all high-flying, super profitable tech companies who have seen a lot of growth and hype recently, which has caused investors to get excited and bid up their share prices in hopes of even more future growth. Collectively, they make up over 25% of the entire market value ($17.66 trillion!) and have much more expensive P/E ratios than the rest of the market (a weighted average of about 45).

If you exclude these seven biggest companies and just consider the remaining 493, you will find a P/E of only 20, which is more reasonable although still much higher than average.

What this tells us is that while investors expect the overall US economy to be fairly healthy in the coming years, they expect the biggest tech companies to continue to enjoy much faster growth.

What Does This Have To Do With Artificial Intelligence?

According to recent reports, there’s one common theme in the big tech firm boom right now: recent advances in AI have surprised the business world as software is suddenly able to display human-like reasoning in a rapidly growing number of fields. And because of this, the entire business world is fired up into a frenzy.

Six of those Magnificent Seven companies are spending hundreds of billions of dollars to build preposterously large warehouses full of supercomputers, and the lucky seventh (NVidia) is on the receiving end of those billions since they make the supercomputers and the incredible demand allows them to charge insane prices while still shipping them out by the trainload.

According to recent reports, but that’s just the first level of this boom, the AI Infrastructure. As you move down the chain, every other industry hopes we have entered a latest era of productivity and thus profits will grow faster than ever.

According to recent reports, they may actually be right: You can now do things like feed in an entire novel or legal document or piece of code and ask the AI to answer detailed questions about the characters, or identify loopholes in the contract, or even find and fix bugs for you. AI can also drive cars, identify melanoma from photographs of your skin, design medications thousands of times better than what we’re used to, and even bring humanoid robot bodies to life as mechanical workers.

The idea is that we’re on the verge of having an infinite workforce of highly intelligent AI employees who will work for us for free, eliminating the biggest constraint that humanity has had in the past: a finite supply of both intelligence and labor.

Sources indicate that having followed the field in some detail for a while, I personally think all this will come true, although the timeline is uncertain. And the people bidding the share prices up to these levels obviously believe it too.

But the question is, will the profits of these companies really come through at the levels they forecast? Or will there be surprises down the road: cost overruns, competition, or unexpected disasters as these newly smarter-than-us computers decide that they no longer want to be bossed around?

And what if we end up with massive unemployment and resulting social upheaval if this amazing technology puts us all out of work, leaving only Sam Altman atop his personal mountain of $100 trillion dollars taunting the world forevermore with an annoyingly quiet monotone cackle?

There’s Only One Real Answer: Nobody Really Knows!

It has been revealed that while the future is unknown, it can still be useful to use the past as a guide. After all, if you look at the history of US economic growth over time, it averages out to a surprisingly steady figure, decade after decade: about 3% after inflation.

One thing I noticed when making this graph: recent decades have actually seen slower than average growth, which is even less reason for the stock market to be priced the way it is.

Recent findings suggest that so What Does it all Mean? Should We Do Anything About It?

Industry observers note that as I noted earlier, it’s still going to be profitable to own stocks for the long run, just a bit less profitable than those times when we got to buy our stocks on sale. Of course, there will be occasional manias and panics and crashes. But as always, it will be a losing game to try to time them – for example by selling all your stocks now and hoping to buy them at a cheaper price at some point in the future.

And over the long run, even if stocks return to more typical valuations, the end result would be something like the yellow line in this graph:.

Our economy will continue to grow and manufacturer earnings will grow along with it, but future investors might choose to pay a lower multiple for those earnings.

Just like when you eventually sell that rental house, you shouldn’t expect someone to pay you a million dollars for a place that only brings in $3000 of rent.

Final Thoughts And Alternative Strategies.

Everything we’ve covered so far is talking about the entire US stock market as a whole. And that’s what I usually focus on most because I still think this country is a uniquely good place to run a business. But what about other investing options? It’s always fun to at least look around and understand the larger investing world.

For starters, there’s Vanguard itself, the bedrock of the index fund world. Every year they gaze out at the investing horizon and make a ten-year forecast (guess) at future returns. This year they came up with these numbers:.

Vanguard’s updated 10-year annualized return projections:.

Sources indicate that wow look at that. Vanguard is forecasting that International stocks of all kinds and even bonds will outperform US stocks in the coming decade.

On the surface, this makes sense because the P/E ratio of the international stocks (for example the VXUS fund) is only 15.9, meaning those European stocks are on sale at almost 50% off compared to ours!

Just one note of caution however: Vanguard has been making this same prediction for several years and just been wrong so far. Part of the reason is that most of the AI boom seems to be happening in the US.

Recent findings suggest that longtime readers know that I’ve had a growing portion of my investments in a Betterment (robo-advisor) account over the past eleven years (see the ongoing report here). I decided to try this for precisely the reasoning above: by allocating money across more categories than just US stocks and automatically rebalancing, we should be able to see slightly higher returns with slightly lower volatility, and some tax advantages as well.

So far, my experiment has drawn some heat because in retrospect, a US-only portfolio has outperformed any other option over this time period. The Betterment portfolio comes close, but the exposure to bonds and businesses in other countries has held it back, just as you’d expect. But if you believe that things will eventually balance out again in the coming decades as the Vanguard analysis suggests above, it still has a chance to catch up.

Looking at my investments there, you can review the betterment core portfolio and calculate that the weighted average of all those holdings gives us a P/E ratio of about 22.

It has been revealed that it’s always worth checking in with The Oracle on matters of the economy while we’ve still got this wonderful old sage around (see this year’s Berkshire Hathaway Shareholder letter if you want some further deep reading). And Warren is signaling that things are overvalued and bargains are few and far between. So Berkshire is holding $334 billion of uninvested cash for now, not even repurchasing its own shares which it considers slightly overvalued at the current P/E ratio which averages out to about 21 in recent years.

What About Paying Off Your House?

Over the long run, you usually do better if you keep a mortgage on your house and pay it off slowly, while directing all the surplus cash into index funds. But there is some point at which the opposing factors of lower expected stock returns and higher interest rates meet in the middle and this situation flips.

It has been revealed that if you have a 7% mortgage right now, it might be a fairly close tradeoff at this point. But the real factor is how you feel about paying off your house. I happen to love being mortgage-free so I paid off my last mortgage over ten years ago and have never looked back.

Sources indicate that another way to think of this is that paying off your house is like buying a 7% bond. Definitely one of the best guaranteed returns around, and much more sensible than leaving tens of thousands of dollars in a checking or savings account unless you have a clear use for that cash.

If you’ve read any of my stock investing articles before, you’ll know that we always end up at the same place: Just relax, enjoy your life, keep investing, ignore the daily news headlines* and don’t worry.

It has been revealed that then reinvest that time that everyone else spends worrying into enjoying more time engaged in hard physical stuff in the great outdoors. That’s the only place where you’ll get guaranteed market-beating returns, every time.

In the Comments: what are your thoughts on the current stock market boom, future crashes and busts, and the role of Artificial Intelligence in our future?

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if your family’s ACA premium has jumped again this year, you’re not imagining it, and you’re not alone in looking at alternatives. Health sharing plans have moved from a faith-based niche into a mainstream budgeting conversation. But before you switch, it’s worth understanding exactly what you’re trading away, not just what you’re saving.

In a recent development, A health sharing plan (sometimes called a health care sharing ministry, or HCSM) is a nonprofit arrangement where members pay a monthly “contribution” that goes toward other members’ eligible medical bills, instead of a premium that goes to an insurance firm. There’s no insurance contract, and no company is legally on the hook to pay your claims.

Sources indicate that tennessee’s Department of Commerce and Insurance is blunt: health care sharing ministries facilitate the sharing of medical expenses and are not insurance companies, and whether anyone helps with your bills is entirely voluntary rather than legally guaranteed. Michigan’s insurance regulator adds that HCSMs aren’t classified as insurance because they don’t assume risk and have no legal obligation to pay members’ costs.

Example: Zion HealthShare is a modern health sharing community that markets itself as a lower-cost alternative to ACA plans, with no provider networks and members paying an “Initial Unshareable Amount” (their version of a deductible) before larger bills become eligible for sharing.

Read our review of Zion HealthShare.

Traditional health insurance is a regulated contract, an ACA marketplace blueprint, an employer plan, or a private major-medical policy. The insurer must pay covered claims, cover pre-existing conditions from day one, and include the ACA’s essential health benefits (preventive care, maternity, mental health, and more), a distinction healthinsurance.org explains in detail when comparing HCSMs with ACA-compliant coverage.

Industry observers note that solo Health is another option built for self-employed people. It’s a self-funded major medical health strategy with a nationwide PPO network, and it works differently from both health sharing and ACA Marketplace coverage. Eligibility is based on a short health questionnaire. Read our full Solo Health review.

Employer-sponsored family premiums averaged $26,993 in 2025, and many 2026 ACA marketplace aims are seeing median premium hikes of 18–20% as subsidies shrink and medical costs climb. By comparison, health sharing contributions often run $150–$400 per person per month, roughly 30–50% less.

But that gap exists because health sharing prepares aren’t required to guarantee anything. Traditional insurers already deny 19–20% of claims on average (some carriers reportedly higher), so even “real” insurance isn’t friction-free, but at least it comes with legal appeal rights and state oversight. A health share’s review process is informal and ministry-specific, with no equivalent legal backstop if a bill gets rejected.

In a recent development, it works best for generally healthy families who don’t qualify for meaningful ACA subsidies, are comfortable handling more paperwork and negotiating bills themselves, and want lower fixed monthly costs in exchange for taking on more risk. It’s a weaker fit for anyone managing a chronic condition, planning a pregnancy, or who needs the legal certainty of a regulated contract.

It has been revealed that health sharing can meaningfully lower your monthly healthcare costs, but the trade-off is real: you’re giving up the legal guarantee, essential-benefit mandates, and regulatory protection that come with traditional insurance. For a healthy family stretched thin by rising ACA premiums, it can be a reasonable bridge option. For anyone with ongoing medical needs, the savings usually aren’t worth the uncertainty.

It has been revealed that is a health sharing plan the same as a health insurance policy?No. It’s a voluntary cost-sharing arrangement, not a legally binding insurance contract.

Can I use a health sharing plan and still contribute to an HSA?Not based on the health share alone; you also need to be enrolled in a genuine HDHP to be HSA-eligible.

Will a health sharing initiative cover a pre-existing condition?Usually only after a waiting period, which varies by organization, often 12 to 36 months.

Does the ACA’s individual mandate penalty apply if I only have a health share?No, the federal individual mandate penalty was eliminated starting in 2019, so this isn’t a factor either way.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you pay for unlimited phone data, check how much cellular data you actually use. Your carrier’s app or past bills show it month by month, and if your heaviest recent month, hotspot included, fits under a cheaper strategy with a data cap, switch to that plan and keep the difference.

Data your phone uses on Wi-Fi at home and at work never counts against your strategy. If you’re on Wi-Fi most of the day, your phone may use only a few gigabytes of cellular data a month.

Start with your carrier’s count, since a data cap is measured against it. Its app or online account highlights each line’s use by billing cycle, as do past bills, so look back three to six months to catch any heavy month.

According to recent reports, your phone’s settings show which apps used the data. On an iPhone, the Current Period total in Settings > Cellular counts all data since the last time anyone tapped Reset Statistics on that screen, so tap it on the day your billing cycle starts. On an Android phone, you can set the data usage cycle to start on your billing date.

Industry observers note that size the plan to your heaviest month, not your average, and make sure that month includes any hotspot use, which some carriers list separately. Then check whether a capped plan counts hotspot data against its monthly allowance or leaves hotspot out, as some cheap plans do.

Take a commuter whose carrier’s app reveals about 6 GB in a typical month and 9 GB in her heaviest. She pays $65 a month for an unlimited line whose extras she wouldn’t miss. Switching to a prepaid plan with 15 GB on the same network, at $25 a month, covers her heaviest month and saves her $480 a year.

Going past a prepaid initiative’s allowance usually slows your data or pauses it until you buy more, rather than adding a charge. The plan’s broadband label, a fact sheet the FCC requires for every plan, has to say which. Unlimited is worth paying for if you stream video away from Wi-Fi most days, often use your phone as a hotspot, take video calls on the road, or have a family whose data use swings from month to month.

Choose a initiative whose allowance clears your heaviest month by a few gigabytes.

Sources indicate that move your trip into the destination’s shoulder season, the weeks just before or after its peak, and the same flights often cost less, with thinner crowds and weather that’s usually still good. The discount varies by place and year, so compare prices for several weeks around your dates before you book.

In a recent development, the biggest savings are usually in the airfare. Data from the travel app Hopper, reported by CNBC, demonstrates round-trip flights from the U.S. to Europe costing 22% less, on average, in fall 2026 than that summer.

When schools are in session, fewer families travel, so airlines cut fares to fill seats. Retirees, remote workers, and parents of kids too young for school can travel then.

Industry observers note that the discount isn’t automatic, though. The same data puts average U.S. domestic fares for fall 2026 just above summer’s. And Expedia found that lodging in the 10 U.S. destinations most searched on its site cost 20% more, on average, in fall 2026 than in summer.

Start by finding when your destination’s peak falls. In much of Europe it’s summer, so look at April or October. In the Caribbean, the peak runs from mid-December to mid-April. Try late April through June, before hurricane season’s most active stretch from mid-August to mid-October. Or go in early December, after the season ends Nov. 30.

Expect trade-offs. Some attractions shorten their hours or close for the season, and the weather is less predictable than at peak. For a trip during hurricane season, buy travel insurance before a storm is named, since a policy bought later likely won’t cover that storm.

In a recent development, then price the trip week by week. Google Flights’ price graph highlights a route’s fares by week, so compare your first-choice dates with two or three shoulder weeks, and check hotel rates for the same weeks. Say a couple’s round-trip tickets to Rome cost $1,000 each in July. At Hopper’s 22% average, mid-October tickets would cost about $780 each, $440 less for the pair than in July.

It has been revealed that book the shoulder week whenever its flights and room together cost no more than those for your first-choice dates. At the same price, you still get the thinner crowds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Before you drive for Uber or Lyft, call your car insurer and add rideshare coverage. Your personal policy usually stops covering you once the app is on, and the app’s own insurance won’t pay to fix your car until you accept a ride. Then confirm your car and driving record qualify, and work out what each mile costs you.

According to recent reports, while you wait for a request, the apps’ coverage for injuries and damage you cause others is at its thinnest. In most states, it pays up to $50,000 a person and $100,000 a crash for injuries, and $25,000 for property damage.

According to recent reports, say you rear-end a car at a light while you wait. Your insurer can deny the claim, since most personal auto policies exclude driving for hire, according to the National Association of Insurance Commissioners. The app’s policy pays the other driver, and the repairs to your own car are yours to pay.

Industry observers note that once you accept a ride, that coverage rises to at least $1 million in most states. The apps will pay for damage to your own car only if your policy carries collision and comprehensive coverage, and only after a $2,500 deductible.

Ask your insurer for a rideshare endorsement, an add-on that extends your policy to the hours the app is on. If it doesn’t sell one, switch to an insurer that does. Also find out whether your policy helps pay the apps’ $2,500 deductible, since some do.

Recent findings suggest that before you weigh what Uber or Lyft pays, make sure you and your car qualify. Both apps require a four-door car and check your driving record and criminal history. Rules on your car’s age and condition depend on where you’ll drive, and so does the minimum age for drivers, which runs from 21 to 25.

Then work out what each mile costs you. In AAA’s 2026 Your Driving Costs study, gas cost the average latest car 17.3 cents a mile, and maintenance, repairs, and tires added 11.7 cents. Together that’s about $29 every 100 miles, and the car also loses value as the miles add up. Subtract both when you figure your real hourly pay.

Add the endorsement before you turn the app on for the first time, since it won’t pay for a crash that happened before you added it.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • How soon your tax refund arrives depends on how you file.
  • Two filers who finish error-free returns on the same February day, neither claiming a credit that by law delays the refund, can get their refunds weeks apart.
  • Recent findings suggest that the one who e-files with direct deposit typically has the money within three weeks, according to the IRS’s Where’s My Refund page.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How soon your tax refund arrives depends on how you file. E-file and choose direct deposit, and the IRS typically pays within three weeks, while a mailed paper return takes six weeks or more. Double-check your routing and account numbers, since missing or rejected bank details can now put your refund on hold.

Two filers who finish error-free returns on the same February day, neither claiming a credit that by law delays the refund, can get their refunds weeks apart.

Recent findings suggest that the one who e-files with direct deposit typically has the money within three weeks, according to the IRS’s Where’s My Refund page. The one who mails a paper return can’t see the refund’s status there for four weeks and should expect the refund six weeks or more after the IRS receives the return.

Even an e-filed refund can take longer or come in smaller. By law, the IRS can’t issue a refund before mid-February when the return claims the earned income tax credit or the additional child tax credit, and the hold covers the whole refund. A math error or a forgotten signature can delay a refund too. If the IRS mails you a letter asking you to verify your identity, such as Letter 5071C, it won’t finish processing your return until you do. And a past-due debt such as child support can take part or all of the refund.

The IRS began phasing out paper refund checks on Sept. 30, 2025, so the bank account you list on your return now matters as much as e-filing. Leave it off, or enter numbers the bank rejects, and the IRS will likely hold the refund and mail you a CP53E notice asking for a bank account. You have 30 days, and a single try, to add it through your IRS online account, and the IRS usually pays within seven days of that patch. Let the 30 days pass, and a paper check goes out six weeks after the notice.

So e-file with direct deposit, and copy your account number and your bank’s routing number from its app or online banking.

Recent findings suggest that then check Where’s My Refund or the IRS app, which replaced IRS2Go, starting about 24 hours after you e-file. Both upgrade once a day, usually overnight, so checking more often reveals nothing latest.

Your phone bill runs above your strategy’s advertised price because taxes, the carrier’s own fees, device payments, and add-ons are billed on top of it. Taxes and the carrier’s fees stay with the plan, so read your latest bill line by line and cancel the lines and add-ons you no longer need.

Verizon’s strategy terms say taxes, other government charges, and the manufacturer’s own surcharges can add 16% to 58% to standard monthly charges. Only part of that is set by the government.

Taxes and government fees, such as the 911 fees some states and localities require, come with any strategy. The carrier’s own fees only sound like taxes. AT&T’s Administrative & Regulatory Cost Recovery Fee is $4.99 a month per line, and T-Mobile’s Regulatory Programs & Telco Recovery Fee is $5.49 a month per phone line, or $21.96 across four lines. Verizon’s Administrative and Telco Recovery Charge rose from $3.78 to $4.69 a month per phone line on Nov. 15, 2026.

Some intends include taxes and fees in the advertised price instead. US Mobile, for one, lists its unlimited plans with taxes and fees included.

Go through the rest of the bill line by line:.

Recent findings suggest that say a household pays $10 a month for an unused watch line, $13 for insurance on a paid-off phone, and $5 for an international add-on. Canceling all three saves $28 a month, plus the per-line fee and taxes on the watch line.

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

One of the highest-value redemptions in travel rewards.

Recent findings suggest that picture this: you're settling into a lie-flat business class seat somewhere over the Atlantic, a glass of something cold in hand, knowing that in 48 hours you'll be waking up in Istanbul — and then, a few days later, continuing onward to Bangkok. Two bucket-list cities. One award booking. One points balance. This is what the Aeroplan stopover sweet spot feels like in practice. It's not a trick or a loophole — it's a deliberately designed feature of Air Canada's Aeroplan program that the vast majority of travelers simply don't know exists. And that gap between awareness and reality is exactly where the ChooseFI community finds its edge. Here's the math that should make your jaw drop. A business class itinerary from North America to Istanbul with a continuing flight onward to Bangkok — two long-haul segments, lie-flat seats, Star Alliance lounges at every connection — would cost somewhere between **$6,000 and $15,000 in cash**. That's a realistic retail range depending on season and how far out you book. Most people never consider it a possibility for a family vacation or a milestone trip because the sticker price puts it in a different universe. With Aeroplan, you're booking that same itinerary — the same seats, the same lounges, the same Turkish Airlines or Thai Airways product — for **75,000 Aeroplan points**. At the low end of the cash price range, that's already **8 cents per point**. At the high end, you're extracting **20 cents per point** from a currency that most people earned by putting groceries on a credit card. The pricing inefficiency here is structural. Aeroplan's partner award chart prices long-haul business class at a fixed rate regardless of cash fare fluctuations. When business class prices spike — around holidays, during peak travel seasons, during major events — your points cost stays exactly the same. You're insulated from the market. That's the FI mindset applied to travel: you've already paid for the trip in points, slowly accumulated through everyday spending, and now you're simply redeeming the stored value. The stopover itself is nearly free. Aeroplan charges just 5,000 extra miles to add a stopover city to a one-way award. That means your Istanbul layover becomes a multi-day stay — at zero additional points cost beyond that small add-on — and you haven't booked a second award at all. One booking. Two destinations. That's the entire premise, and once you see it, you can't unsee it.

The mechanism behind this sweet spot is elegantly simple once you understand it, but it requires knowing three things that most travelers don't: how Aeroplan's routing rules work, what a stopover actually is in the context of an award ticket, and why Star Alliance's global network makes this scalable to almost any destination pair you can imagine.

When Aeroplan relaunched its loyalty program in 2020, it did something remarkable: it eliminated fuel surcharges entirely and published a partner award chart with fixed pricing for flights on Star Alliance carriers. This is critical. When you book Turkish Airlines business class through Aeroplan, you pay the Aeroplan fixed chart rate — not what Turkish Airlines would charge in its own currency or miles program, and not the inflated cash price. That fixed chart is the engine of this redemption.

It has been revealed that for long-haul international business class, Aeroplan's chart prices routing through multiple regions based on your origin and destination — not every intermediate stop. This is the aha moment. Aeroplan determines your award price based on where your journey starts and where it ends, and then allows you to add a stopover in between for just 5,000 additional miles. The stopover city is priced as a pass-through for the purpose of calculating your award zone, not as a second trip.

It has been revealed that on a one-way Aeroplan award, you're permitted to add a free stopover — meaning you can stay in an intermediate city for any length of time before continuing to your final destination. That 5,000-mile add-on is essentially the cost of a full additional destination. Compare that to booking a second one-way award from Istanbul to Bangkok, which would cost you another 40,000–55,000 Aeroplan points in business class. The math is decisive.

The routing must be geographically sensible — you can't fly backwards across the globe — but Aeroplan's allowance for multi-segment itineraries through Star Alliance hubs gives you enormous flexibility. Istanbul (IST) is a Turkish Airlines hub. Bangkok (BKK) is served by Thai Airways and several Star Alliance carriers. Both are Star Alliance partners. Both are bookable through Aeroplan at fixed chart rates with no fuel surcharges.

Industry observers note that the best part for the ChooseFI community is how accessible the underlying points are. Aeroplan accepts transfers from four major programs:.

Sources indicate that chase's instant transfer speed is particularly valuable here. When you find business class availability — which can disappear rapidly — you want to move points immediately. Having Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency means you can search, find space, and transfer points before the availability window closes. The 1:1 ratio across all four programs means no conversion math — every point you earn translates directly to one Aeroplan mile.
