Recent findings suggest that booking an Aeroplan stopover award in business class is genuinely one of the more complex redemptions in the travel rewards world, but it becomes manageable when you break it into distinct phases. Here's exactly how to do it.

Start by deciding on your two destinations. Aeroplan stopovers work best when your intermediate city is a major Star Alliance hub that lies geographically between your origin and final destination. Classic combinations include North America to Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub) continuing to Southeast Asia, or North America to a European hub continuing to the Middle East or East Africa. Your stopover city should be somewhere you genuinely want to spend 2–5 days — this is a real trip, not just a layover.

This is the most key and most time-consuming step. You need to find saver-level business class availability on both segments independently before you book.

Once you've confirmed availability on both segments, go to aeroplan.com and use the multi-city search function. Enter your full itinerary — origin, stopover city with your intended layover dates, and final destination.

Once you've confirmed the award is bookable and are ready to complete the reservation:.

Complete your booking on aeroplan.com or with a phone agent, confirm the stopover is properly reflected in your itinerary, and save every confirmation email. Verify your seats on each carrier's website immediately after booking.

A stopover is an intentional break in your journey lasting more than 24 hours at a connecting city. Most airlines treat stopovers as separate tickets, charging full price for each segment. Aeroplan is one of the few programs that allows a free stopover on round-trip awards, letting you explore a connecting city for days before continuing to your final destination. This is fundamentally different from a layover, which is a brief connection of a few hours at an airport. The stopover must be in a city served by a Star Alliance carrier on your routing, and the key is that Aeroplan prices the entire itinerary as one award, not two.

Let's build a real example so you can see exactly what this looks like on paper — and in the air.

The Route: Toronto (YYZ) → Istanbul (IST, 4-day stopover) → Bangkok (BKK) The Carrier: Turkish Airlines business class on both segments The Points Cost: 75,000 Aeroplan miles for the two segments + 5,000 miles for the stopover = 80,000 Aeroplan miles total Cash Equivalent: A comparable business class itinerary on this routing typically retails for $9,000–$12,000 in 2026, depending on when you search and how far in advance you book.

The CPP Calculation: At the midpoint cash value of $10,500 against 80,000 points, you're extracting 13.1 cents per Aeroplan mile — well inside the 8–20 cent range this sweet spot delivers, and roughly 10–13 times the value of redeeming Aeroplan miles for cash back.

Recent findings suggest that the Turkish Airlines business class product on long-haul routes is consistently rated among the top business class experiences in the Star Alliance network. On the YYZ–IST segment — operated on a 787 or A330 — you'll have access to a lie-flat seat with direct aisle access, the Turkish Airlines Lounge in Istanbul (widely considered one of the best airport lounges in the world, full stop), and a meal service that reflects the airline's culinary reputation. The IST lounge alone — with its restaurant, spa, golf simulator, and sleeping areas — is worth lingering in even before your onward connection.

According to recent reports, in Istanbul, your four days might include the Hagia Sophia at sunrise, a Bosphorus dinner cruise, and the Grand Bazaar before you head to the airport to continue your journey. You've paid nothing additional for this stay beyond the 5,000-mile stopover fee.

The IST–BKK segment puts you into Bangkok in the evening, ready for Thailand's extraordinary food, culture, and cost of living — which, for the FI-minded traveler, means your lodging and meals on the ground are remarkably affordable, stretching the value of your trip even further.

Total points cost for two lie-flat business class segments and a full European city stay: 80,000 miles, earned on everyday credit card spending. That's the entire proposition, and those numbers are real.

Book at exactly 355 days out. Aeroplan opens its booking window at 355 days before departure. The best business class availability on popular routes — especially Turkish Airlines long-haul — appears at this window and gets claimed promptly. Set a calendar reminder and be ready to search at the 355-day mark for your target travel dates.

In a recent development, use Chase Ultimate Rewards as your primary earning currency for this redemption. The instant transfer speed to Aeroplan is genuinely differentiating. When you find award space and need to move swiftly, Chase lets you transfer and book in the same session. Amex, Capital One, and Bilt all require 1–2 days, during which your availability can evaporate.

Recent findings suggest that search availability before you transfer points. Confirm space exists on every segment before a single point moves. There's no undo button on a transfer, and Aeroplan points sitting idle in your account are fine — points transferred to an account where you can't find availability are a headache.

Call Aeroplan for complex routings. The online multi-city tool is functional but can struggle with nuanced stopover configurations. Phone agents are experienced with these bookings and have the same access to inventory. The call is worth it for an $80,000-point booking.

Leverage the open-jaw rule too. Aeroplan also allows open-jaw routing — fly into one city, depart from another. Combined with the stopover, you can design a route that visits three geographic points on a single award: fly into Istanbul, take trains or ferries to Athens, and fly home from Athens. The award prices the same way.

Recent findings suggest that don't assume partner availability matches Aeroplan's search. Turkish Airlines and other Star Alliance partners don't always make every seat available through Aeroplan's online portal. If you see space on the carrier's own site but not on aeroplan.com, call — agents can often access inventory the website misses.

According to recent reports, don't book inflexible connecting flights. Long-haul itineraries with tight connections are a risk. Build in at least a 3-hour connection at hub airports to protect against irregular operations that could affect your award segments.

Industry observers note that don't earn Marriott Bonvoy® points with this redemption in mind. The 3:1 transfer ratio to Aeroplan makes Marriott a poor choice for funding this specific award. Stick to Amex, Chase, Capital One, or Bilt at 1:1.

Don't book this for a time-sensitive trip. Award availability, transfer timelines, and multi-carrier coordination mean this requires planning runway. Build in at least 3–4 weeks of lead time beyond the actual booking date.

This redemption is purpose-built for the advanced travel rewards enthusiast in the ChooseFI community — someone who has already mastered the basics (earning transferable points, understanding award charts, booking straightforward partner awards) and is ready to unlock the next level of value.

The ideal profile: A couple or solo traveler planning a milestone trip — a significant anniversary, a sabbatical, a once-in-a-decade adventure — who wants to experience two destinations in business class without paying business class prices for either one. You're flexible on travel dates, comfortable spending time on the phone with an airline agent, and genuinely excited about the trip-planning process as part of the experience.

Industry observers note that minimum points balance: You'll need approximately 80,000 Aeroplan miles to complete this booking (75,000 for the award plus 5,000 for the stopover). That's achievable from a single premium credit card welcome bonus, a combination of two or three mid-tier welcome bonuses, or 12–18 months of everyday spending on a 2x transferable points card.

Pick a final destination and a stopover city on the same Star Alliance routing. Classic combos: Istanbul + Bangkok, Zurich + Tokyo, Vienna + Singapore. The stopover city must be a natural connection point on a Star Alliance route between your origin and destination.

Set a calendar alert for 355 days before your departure date. Search for business class availability on each segment separately using United.com or Aeroplan.com. Both legs need saver-level award space on the same booking.

Recent findings suggest that before transferring any points, verify that saver award space exists on both the outbound leg (origin to stopover city) and the continuation (stopover city to final destination). If either segment is unavailable, the booking will not work.

Transfer Chase Ultimate Rewards (instant) or Amex Membership Rewards (1-2 days) to your Aeroplan account at a 1:1 ratio. Only transfer once you have confirmed availability on both segments.

Call Aeroplan or use the multi-city search tool online. Specify your stopover city and duration (up to the maximum allowed). The system prices it as one round-trip award. Confirm total points match expectations before completing the booking.

Recent findings suggest that aeroplan allows stopovers of up to 45 days on round-trip awards. You can stay in your stopover city for a few days or several weeks, giving you genuine time to explore rather than just passing through.

Recent findings suggest that no, stopovers are only available on round-trip awards through Aeroplan. One-way bookings do not qualify for the free stopover benefit. This is one reason round-trip awards can offer better value than two one-ways.

In a recent development, aeroplan has improved its online multi-city search tool, and some stopover itineraries can now be booked online. However, complex routings may still require a phone call. When calling, clearly state you want a round-trip award with a stopover and specify your stopover city and dates.

It has been revealed that the best stopover cities are Star Alliance hub cities with strong business class availability: Istanbul (Turkish Airlines hub), Zurich (SWISS hub), Vienna (Austrian hub), Singapore (Singapore Airlines hub), and Tokyo (ANA hub). These hubs offer the most consistent saver-level award space.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

It has been revealed that the Aeroplan stopover is one of the most powerful tools in the travel rewards playbook. By adding a free stopover to a round-trip business class award, you can explore two world-class cities for the points cost of visiting one. It requires planning, patience at the 355-day booking window, and comfort with Star Alliance routing rules, but the payoff is extraordinary: 10-15 cents per point in value on experiences that would cost thousands in cash. For the FI community member who has mastered basic award bookings and is ready to level up, this is the redemption that changes how you think about travel.

Tech Report: How to Navigate the Tariff Circus

📅 13 Jun 2025 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2437 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well.
  • And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.
  • As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that quite accidentally, it looks like we timed our last talk about the stock market pretty darned well. Back in February 2025, the market put the perfect cap on a multi year climb before stepping onto the wild roller coaster we’re presently riding. Since then it has seen some of the steepest drops and recoveries in history, losing a full 20% of its value at the bottom while somehow managing to end up right back near the peak as I’m writing this.

And although stock market volatility doesn’t always come with an easily labeled explanation, this time the reason seems pretty clear: it’s the Tariffs.

As our financial world has been whipped around like a circus tent in a hurricane for the last several months, almost everyone who has a stake in this country has been wondering what to make of it.

Sources indicate that as I write this, we still don’t know the outcome of the worldwide tariff and trade battle that our unpredictable government has unleashed upon the world. But we’re already seeing the results: businesses are bracing for massive changes, currencies and interest rates are reacting, and regular investors like you and me are wondering what the future holds for our early retirement funds. Surveying my own group of friends, the reactions span the whole range of emotions from “this is a giant Nothingburger” to “we’re all totally screwed.”.

So what’s the real answer? To get closer to that, we should start with the most basic question of:.

Industry observers note that A tariff is just a sales tax charged by our government on goods which are imported into the country. They are paid by whoever is doing the importing – meaning you if you order something like an e-bike directly from a organization in China, or by companies like Amazon, Walmart, or Apple which import products from other countries by the shipload.

Sources indicate that but in the end, the tariffs aren’t paid by China or Amazon or Apple. They are paid by you, the end consumer, because if their cost of goods increases, a retailer is of course going to raise their prices to continue to make a profit.

Tariffs also affect companies directly: if Home Depot wants to build a upcoming store or Chevron needs a new oil rig, the tariffs on imported steel, copper, lumber and a million other components will raise the cost of these construction projects. And they raise the cost of housing, because most of the building materials in houses come from multiple countries as well.

In a recent development, on average, tariffs will result in higher prices for everything just like any other broad-based sales tax. And just like most other taxes, the overall effect is to slow the economy and reduce our spending power. On the positive side, all that tax money flows into the government’s pocket which could help fund the national budget and even reduce the deficit.

According to recent reports, of course, every government needs at least some tax revenue to function, so it makes sense to use some mix of sales, income and corporate taxes to get there. The most important part is that the levels need to be as low as possible while still keeping the country running well, and as fair and predictable as possible, so that people and businesses have an incentive to work hard and the ability to blueprint far into the future.

And that’s where our current tariff regime gets it completely backwards. Donald Trump is throwing around random, extremely high tariff numbers as threats, then walking them back and changing them on an almost daily basis..

Whoa, that Sounds Mostly Bad – Is There a Good Side of Tariffs?

Recent findings suggest that sometimes, a country will use tariffs to protect their own domestic industries. For example, if you put a tax on imported Hondas, then General Motors cars will gain a competitive advantage – so GM will make more money. In this example, most consumers end up losing due to increased prices and decreased selection. But at least domestic auto manufacturers and their employees are happy.

This can be strategic (for example we might want to slap a tax on imported fighter jets to make sure Boeing and Lockheed can remain in business, for national defense purposes.) Or it can be corrupt (a politician might receive funding from kingpins in the steel industry, and in return then push through tariffs on imported steel to protect the profits of US steelmakers.).

And this isn’t just a Trump or Republican thing either – Joe Biden used tariffs during his terms in an attempt to please swing-state voters. One of the worst examples was a tax on imported solar panel components (which Trump has since raised even further, proving that Boneheadedness can be Bipartisan). These are sheets of cheap glass that literally pump the cheapest energy and easiest wealth into your country for 30 years as soon as you plug them in. Cheap energy lowers everyone’s cost of living while also boosting industry. There is no good reason to block such wealth from flowing across your borders.

Can Tariffs Bring Us More Jobs?

Let’s go back to that hypothetical tax on Hondas, and let’s say it’s a massive one like $5000. At that level, many buyers will start heading over to the GM dealer next door to consider what he’s selling. Sure, the GM cars may not be as good, but for five grand some people are going to settle in order to save some money.

Because of this, GM’s sales go up. So they hire more employees and build more factories. They might even develop some latest models and new technologies in response to all that new demand. More people learn advanced skills and in the best case it becomes a virtuous circle.

It has been revealed that but in exchange for this boom in the auto industry, everyone else has to pay more for slightly shittier cars and trucks. Higher vehicle prices means Amazon will have to spend more on their delivery fleet, so they will raise prices slightly on everything they sell. Somewhere a startup company or a medical breakthrough will be just a bit less likely to happen, because they are operating in an environment that is just a bit more expensive and a bit less efficient.

According to recent reports, on top of that, with GM liberated from the hassle of competing with Honda, it will have less incentive to innovate and streamline itself. So its overall trajectory will be slower and less efficient even if its profits are higher.

Industry observers note that this big picture effect is why most economists agree that tariffs should be used very sparingly. They almost always cause unexpected damage, decrease overall employment and slow down an economy, but sometimes (like for food security or national defense) those costs are worth paying.

So Why is Donald Trump Throwing Around Tariffs Like They Are The Best Thing Ever?

This has been confusing to almost everyone. If you take him at his word, he appears to have a Bizarro Opposite Universe belief system about economics. Donald has claimed in speeches that the tariffs will somehow make us wealthier. He’s focusing on the first-order effects like GM hiring more workers, while completely ignoring the fact that everything else in the country gets less efficient in exchange.

But when he announces larger tariffs, share prices go down, because everyone who actually runs or invests in US companies knows that of course they will make less money on average. When tariffs are paused or reduced, share prices go back up. Yet he keeps wielding the threats and we go back and forth.

It seems to be obvious to everyone except Donald himself that Tariffs are just a national sales tax rather than some clever sneaky strategic weapon, which leads to various theories that okay, maybe he knows that too but is just pretending in order to gain some influence.

The basic theory goes like this:.

Industry observers note that so right now our entire economy is subject to the whims of a single person.. And as long as this is the case, we’re just the same as any other dictatorship – something our constitution was supposed to prevent with the whole “three independent branches of government” thing.

But presidents have tried to break out of their constitutional cage and get more power many times in the past, and this is just the latest example. The real test will be if our system eventually manages to stop this abuse and put itself back in balance as it always has in the past. You can already see this fight beginning to play out in our court system, in this Economist article:.

How Big are the Tariffs Right Now?

Even without the 145% nonsense numbers that were thrown around a few months ago, they are still far higher than they have been in the last 75 years or more. While it would be hard to pin down the current numbers in a stationary blog post like this one, the key thing to remember is that our current US economy is built around very low tariffs and relatively free trade.

Why haven’t I noticed Prices Going Up Yet?

While the US economy is fueled by a constant stream of cargo ships, as a whole we function like the biggest cargo ship of all: we have a huge inventory and it takes a while to change directions.

In a recent development, so in normal times, we already have several months of inventory of most things in the country. And then when all this drama started, importers started placing even more orders to stockpile things in advance before the tariffs hit. And now that they are in place, we’re importing a lot less stuff.

Industry observers note that for now, we’re still using up the stockpiled inventory, but imports have dropped significantly so we’re rapidly running out of cheap goods. If that happens, we will probably start seeing shortages and price increases throughout this summer or fall. For some things like plastic party trinkets, we can do just fine without. But if we lose access to core useful things like tools and machinery, the economic consequences will be much less fun.

The Dark Side and the Bright Side.

Industry observers note that the most important phrase to remember in US politics and economics is the phrase “This too shall pass.” The only mystery right now is that we don’t know exactly how it will pass. So we could sketch out a few scenarios:.

1) The current crazy-high tariffs really do stick around:.

In a recent development, I personally think this is the less likely scenario because nobody really wants it. But just as a thought experiment, it might go something like this:.

2) They do end up being just a negotiating tactic and we go back to mostly low tariffs.

In other words, the best way to win the tariff game is not to play it.

Industry observers note that just as much of US prosperity is built upon our huge population of 330 million people living in 50 states with open borders and no trade restrictions, all (friendly) countries of the world can benefit from the free exchange of goods, services and even people. We’re all human beings and if we treat each other with a collaborative respect, we all grow richer.

Epilogue: Is it Almost Over Already?

According to recent reports, I started writing this article on April 2nd, when Donald declared his “Liberation Day” and the stock market reacted with the biggest drop since 1932. Some people panicked and locked in significant losses despite decades of warnings from your favorite financial bloggers, like this unfortunate soul in the comments to a JL Collins post:.

But as I watched over the next two months, we have bounced our way back up – with each drop in proposed tariffs triggering a corresponding increase in stock prices (a measure of investor enthusiasm of how bright our future looks).

Right now, the US stock market is just about back to its all-time high. This doesn’t match with our current level of tariffs, which are still about seven times higher than they were before the circus opened. But it indicates that investors believe it’s all going to end with a truce and a resumption of free-ish international trade.

In a recent development, if they’re wrong, the roller coaster ride will still have some more fun in store for us. But as long as we eventually end our current experiment in “emergency” tariff dictatorship and get back to functioning as a democracy, things should be just fine in the long run. I’m still 100% invested myself, so that’s where I place my bet.

The Biggest Lesson: Don’t Form Your Opinions Based on News Headlines.

Industry observers note that decades ago in a brighter age of journalism, there may have been a time when headlines were designed primarily to inform us, with just a bit of sizzle and spice to pull in our attention. Unfortunately, nowadays the priorities have flipped where the primary goal is attention, and accuracy carries little or no weight. Even a totally inaccurate article makes money for the publisher.

So while Democrats and Republicans like to do battle over which media sources are biased, in reality they’re all wrong: all click-funded commercial media is biased – sometimes politically but even more importantly biased towards generating outrage and fear, because those generate more money.

There are two solutions to this:.

1) Either ignore the media completely and focus on your own life, or.

2) Become a subject matter expert on things you really care about, and then read the original sources whenever you want to learn about something.

I mostly practice option #1, but as a science and technology nerd I get into #2 in just the areas I find most interesting. And it’s amazing how the more deeply you understand a subject, the more you see just how wrong most media stories are about your area of expertise. Which means they’re probably pretty wrong about almost everything.

So as always, with this lesson learned it’s time to shut down that phone and laptop, exhale all our worries and get back outside with your real-life family and friends. See you in a few months!

Why We Are Not Really All Doomed – the original all-purpose MMM article which explains why we never really have to worry about the long-term economic future.

Borrow them from the library first, and favor authors who invest in low-cost funds over ones selling a shortcut.

A forum thread on FIRE, short for financial independence, retire early, gives you one stranger’s spreadsheet. A book gives you a whole initiative and the reasoning behind it, so you can see where it fits your life and where it doesn’t.

It has been revealed that you don’t need all eight. A book on the math shows how much saving and investing it takes to leave work early, one on the mindset helps you keep at it for years, and one on a single path shows what those years look like. One of each gives you a initiative to test instead of a pile of tips.

Judge any FIRE book you find later by how its author invests. A strategy built on low-cost index funds, which own every stock in a market index, has nothing extra to sell you. One that only works with the author’s course, coaching, or trading system is selling a shortcut.

The eight below start with the math and the mindset, move on to five different paths, and end with a counterpoint on spending.

For more on investing itself, a few investing books for beginners go deeper on index funds, investor behavior, and stock picking.

Industry observers note that before you buy any of them, check what your library card covers, since thousands of libraries lend e-books and audiobooks free through apps such as Libby and hoopla. Then test whichever proposal wins you over against your own numbers, starting with your savings rate, before you change anything at work.

College students have a lot on their plate already, including the need to study to get good grades, participating in any number of on-campus activities and potentially working part-time to have some spending money.

That noted, college students should also focus on their financial future, including steps they can take to build credit before they enter the workforce.

After all, having a credit history and a good credit score can mean being able to rent an apartment, finance a car or take out a loan, whereas having no credit at all can mean sitting on the sidelines until the situation changes.

It has been revealed that fortunately, there are all kinds of ways for young adults to build credit while they’re still in school. Some strategies require a little work on their part, but many are hands-off tasks that you only have to do once.

Make sure your student knows the basic cornerstones of credit building, including the factors that are used to determine credit scores. While factors like fresh credit, length of credit history and credit mix will play a role in their credit later on, the two most notable issues for credit newcomers to focus on include payment history and credit utilization.

Payment history makes up 35% of FICO scores and credit utilization ratio makes up 30% of scores.

Industry observers note that generally speaking, college students and everyone else can score well in these categories by making all bill payments on time and keeping debt levels low. How low?

Most experts recommend keeping credit utilization below 30% at a maximum and below 10% for the best possible results. This means trying to owe less than $300 for every $1,000 in available credit limits at a maximum, but preferably less than $100 for every $1,000 in credit limits.

In a recent development, one step you can personally take to help a child build credit is adding them to your credit card account as an authorized user. This means they will get a credit card in their name and access to your spending limit, but you are legally responsible for any charges they make. Obviously, this move works best when you have excellent credit and a strong history of on-time payments and you strategy to continue using credit responsibly .

While this step can be risky if you’re worried your college student will use their card to overspend, you don’t actually have to give them their physical authorized user credit card.

In fact, they can get credit for your on-time payments whether they have access to a card or not. If you do decide to give them their credit card, you can do so with the agreement they can only use it for emergency expenses.

Sources indicate that your child can build credit faster if they apply for a credit card and get approved for one on their own, yet this can be difficult for students who have no credit history. That said, secured credit cards require a refundable cash deposit as collateral are very easy to get approved for.

It has been revealed that some secured credit cards like the Ambition Card by College Ave even offer cash back1 on every purchase and don’t charge interest2. If your child opts to start building credit with a secured credit card, make sure they understand the best ways to build credit quickly — keeping credit utilization low and paying bills early or on time each month.

While secured credit cards are a good option for students with little to no credit get started on their journey to good credit, there are also credit cards specifically designed for college students. Student credit cards are unsecured cards, meaning they don’t require an upfront cash deposit as collateral, but charge interest on any purchases not paid in full each month.

It has been revealed that many student credit cards offer rewards for spending with no annual fee required as well, although these cards do tend to come with a high APR. The key to getting the most out of a student credit card is having your dependent use it only for purchases they can afford and paying off the balance in its entirety each billing cycle. After all, sky high interest rates don’t really matter when you never carry a balance from one month to the next.

“One of the safest ways for college student to build their credit by learning valuable money skills.”.

While secured cards and student credit cards help young adults build credit with each bill payment they make, other payments they’re making can also help.

Industry observers note that in fact, using an app like Experian Boost can help them get credit for utility bills they’re paying, subscriptions they pay for and even rent payments they’re making. This app is also free to use, and you only have to set up most bill payments in the app once to have them reported to the credit bureaus.

There are also rent-specific apps and tools students can use to get credit for rent payments, although they come with fees. Examples include websites like Rental Kharma and RentReporters.

The Fair Isaac Corporation (FICO) also notes that students can start building credit with their student loans during school, even if they’re not officially required to make payments until six months after graduation with federal student loans.

Their advice is to make interest-only payments on federal student loans along with payments on any private student loans they have during college in order to start having those payments reported to the credit bureaus as soon as possible.

“Making interest-only payments as a student will not only positively affect your credit history but will also keep the interest from capitalizing and adding to your student loan balance,” the agency writes.

Sources indicate that of course, interest capitalization on loans would only be an matter with private student loans and  Federal Direct Unsubsidized Loans since the U.S. Department of Education pays the interest on Direct Subsidized Loans while you’re in school at least half-time, for six months after you graduate and during periods of deferment.

Sources indicate that college students don’t have to wait until they’re done with school to start building credit for the future, and it makes sense to start building positive credit habits early on regardless. Tools like a credit card can help students on their way, whether they opt for a secured credit card or a student card. Other steps like using credit-building apps can also help, and with little effort on the student’s part or on yours.

It has been revealed that either way, the best time to start building credit was a few years ago, and the second best time is now. You can give your student a leg up on the future by helping them build credit so it’s there when they need it.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Fixtures cost the same wherever they sit, so the money a latest layout adds goes into pipes you’ll never see.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, moving a sink, toilet, or shower is one of the priciest changes in a kitchen or bath remodel, since upcoming drain, vent, and supply lines mean opening floors and walls, paying a licensed plumber, and pulling permits. Leave each fixture on the drain it uses now, and spend your budget on what you see instead.

Fixtures cost the same wherever they sit, so the money a latest layout adds goes into pipes you’ll never see.

According to recent reports, drains run on gravity. The International Residential Code, the model code for houses, requires a sink’s or shower’s drain to drop at least a quarter inch for every foot it runs. Over 12 feet, that’s at least 3 inches of drop the floor has to make room for. Each fixture also needs a vent pipe nearby, so a long move can mean running a latest one up through a wall.

The toilet is the hardest to move, since its drain must be at least 3 inches wide. Under a wood floor, rerouting that pipe can mean cutting and reinforcing joists. On a concrete slab, the floor has to be cut open and patched for any move.

So change what you see and leave the pipes where they are. A latest toilet fits the old drain when it matches the rough-in, the distance from the wall to the drain’s center. A vanity, counters, tile, lighting, and paint all go in around the pipes you have. The same code’s list of work exempt from permits includes painting, tile, cabinets, and countertops. A relocated drain or supply pipe needs a permit and an inspection before the walls close.

It has been revealed that say a bid for a slab-floor bathroom adds $9,500 to put the toilet and a upcoming shower on the far wall. Leaving the toilet alone and setting the shower in the tub’s spot, on a base made to drain where the tub did, keeps that $9,500 for the parts you see.

Sources indicate that move a fixture only when the layout fails you every day, like a kitchen sink with no counter beside it. Even then, keep the move to a few feet, toward the existing drain and vent.

Before you sign, have every bidder price the job twice, with each fixture where it is and with your new layout, so you see what the move alone costs.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • With private insurance, the No Surprises Act keeps an air ambulance from charging you more than an in-network one would, as long as your initiative covers emergency care.
  • People in 22 states had some protection from surprise ground ambulance bills as of February 2026, the Commonwealth Fund found.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, the No Surprises Act protects you from surprise air ambulance bills but not ground ambulance bills. Before you pay a ground ambulance bill, check whether your state caps it, make sure your insurer processed the ride as an emergency, and ask the ambulance service for a discount or payment plan.

With private insurance, the No Surprises Act keeps an air ambulance from charging you more than an in-network one would, as long as your initiative covers emergency care. What you owe a ground ambulance depends on your state’s law, which may cap the bill at what an in-network ambulance would charge you.

People in 22 states had some protection from surprise ground ambulance bills as of February 2026, the Commonwealth Fund found. But states can’t regulate self-funded employer prepares, where the employer pays claims from its own funds, and 71% of workers with job-based coverage are in such a plan, according to KFF’s 2026 Employer Health Benefits Survey.

Industry observers note that say your state limits you to what an in-network ride would cost and your plan’s in-network ambulance copay is $150. A $1,800 bill for the part your insurer didn’t pay then drops to $150.

Use ExpertFlyer alerts to monitor availability passively. 2. **Use Citi ThankYou for instant transfers** so you can act immediately when you find a seat. 3. **Practice the phone booking process** once before your high-stakes redemption — call LifeMiles with a simple question to understand their system. If you've successfully booked one or two simpler awards before, you can absolutely do this. The ChooseFI community has members completing this redemption every year — and every single one indicates the boarding moment made the effort completely worth it.

United indicates Star Alliance partner availability that LifeMiles can book. Search for Saver-level awards in business or first class on your target route. Note the exact carrier, flight number, and date.

Amex MR, Chase UR, Citi ThankYou, and Capital One miles all transfer to LifeMiles. Amex transfers are often fastest (same day). Transfer only after confirming availability in Step 2.

In a recent development, premium cabin award space is limited and competitive. Once your transferred miles appear in your LifeMiles account, complete the booking immediately. Do not wait — the seat can be taken by another searcher.

According to recent reports, lifeMiles charges low taxes and fees on most partner awards, typically $30-$100 depending on the route. Some carriers (notably British Airways) add fuel surcharges, but most Star Alliance carriers keep fees minimal through LifeMiles.

Yes, Lufthansa First Class is bookable through LifeMiles at 87,000 miles one-way from the US to Europe. Availability is limited and typically released at 14 days before departure for partner programs, though some space appears further out. Search on United.com first to confirm Lufthansa First saver space exists before transferring.

It has been revealed that transfer times vary by partner. Amex Membership Rewards transfers often post same-day. Chase Ultimate Rewards transfers typically take 1-2 business days. Citi ThankYou and Capital One transfers can take 1-3 days. Always account for transfer time when booking time-sensitive award space.

Sources indicate that most Star Alliance carriers booked through LifeMiles have low or no fuel surcharges. The notable exception is British Airways (a oneworld carrier, not bookable through LifeMiles). Taxes and fees on typical Star Alliance routes run $30-$100 per ticket, making LifeMiles one of the cheapest programs for out-of-pocket award costs.

If the booking fails because award space disappeared between your search and transfer, the miles sit in your LifeMiles account. They do not expire as long as you have account activity every 12 months. You can use them for a future booking, but you cannot transfer them back to your original program.

Sources indicate that this sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

Avianca LifeMiles is the program that lets FI-community travelers fly the same premium cabins as frequent business travelers at a fraction of the points cost. By consistently underpricing Star Alliance awards, LifeMiles turns 63,000-87,000 transferable points into experiences worth $8,000 or more. 📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, get two or three itemized bids on the same finished proposal, then set your renovation budget at the bid you pick plus 10% to 20% for hidden problems like rot or old wiring. To stay under it, make every choice before demolition, get each change priced in writing, and pay from savings where you can.

Of the homeowners who renovated in 2025, 37% went over budget, the 2026 U.S. Houzz & Home Study found. More than half of them blamed products or services that cost more than they expected, and 35% had picked pricier materials than they first planned.

A budget built from a finished, priced plan makes both causes less likely. The bid prices what you’ll actually build, and the extra 10% to 20% is there for what nobody can see until the walls are open.

Build the budget in this order:.

It has been revealed that say a couple’s chosen bid for a bathroom remodel is $18,000. They set the budget at $21,000, a $3,000 cushion, and when the crew finds rotted subfloor that adds $1,900, they finish $1,100 under budget without borrowing. Cash saved ahead in a high-yield savings account is the cheapest way to pay, since a personal loan or a loan against your home’s equity adds interest.

Then keep the plan from changing. Before demolition, choose every fixture and material, so you never pick in a hurry once the walls are open. Put each change in writing with its price before the crew starts it, and compare your spending with the plan every week.

Keep the cushion for hidden problems like that rotted subfloor, and pay for any upgrade you want midway by cutting a nice-to-have.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.

How Unlimited Free Stuff from Amazon Almost Ruined My Retirement

📅 07 Oct 2025 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2055 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Mrmoneymustache

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon.
  • In a recent development, “Congratulations!
  • I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, it all started last winter when I innocently posted a review for a heated vest I had bought on Amazon. I was happy with this fun newly introduced way to beat the winter and wanted to share it with others, so I gave it five stars. But soon after I clicked “Submit”, I got an email from Amazon which said something like,.

In a recent development, “Congratulations! You’ve been selected to join Amazon Vine for writing helpful reviews!”.

I was already aware of Amazon Vine since I had seen product reviews from other people in the program – typically called “Vine Voices.” The basic idea of this program is that you can order stuff from Amazon for free, as long as you agree to review at least 80% of the things you order.

“Hey, that’s cool”, I thought, “Who doesn’t like free stuff?

Especially since I’ve already been writing product reviews out of the goodness of my heart – why not be rewarded for it?”.

So without giving it much further thought, I clicked “accept” on their terms and conditions and joined the program.

And so began a saga that has taken me on a surprising journey over the past nine months causing me to:.

Okay, I’ll admit that there were also some upsides. My original idea was partly to save some money, by getting stuff I genuinely would have bought anyway, in a way that sounded fun. And that did happen – I saved at least a few thousand dollars on tools and materials for my construction business and the MMM-HQ Coworking space, for free. Plus, at least some of the motivation for signing up was to put myself through an experiment so I could write this blog article about it. And if you’re reading this, it looks like that happened too.

But I was still surprised at how powerful the combination of small nudges and incentives from Amazon was able to hijack my frugality instincts –  and get me to do a bunch of work that wasn’t really the best use of my time.

So I figured if we review my journey and break it down with a bit of Behavioral Science, we could all learn a few valuable things by laughing at Mr. Money Mustache’s folly.

Scarcity Brain and the Online Casino Effect.

One of the most interesting books I’ve read in recent years is Michael Easter’s Scarcity Brain. It’s an exploration of the sneaky ways that modern gambling platforms, marketing and social media algorithms are all built upon two weaknesses in our evolutionary programming:.

As I look back now, I realize that I fell straight into those same traps, because the Vine program has all the key properties of a casino or a TikTok feed:.

But occasionally, there will be genuinely useful things like super nice light fixtures, tools and plumbing parts, an EV charger, and even some clothing. My favorite ridiculous Eagle shirt as featured in the Mustachianism music video was an Amazon Vine find.

As were a whole supply of super-realistic artificial plants, which while tacky in principle, have been amazing for hard-to-water courtyard garden areas at the MMM HQ.

I also had a lot of fun roping in friends and coworkers from HQ to help and share in the bounty. I let them help me request and review stuff that they wanted, and then they got to keep it. This seemed like a win/win because we shared the work and the fun of laughing at some of the ridiculous products available.

Still, as I went through this experiment this spring and summer and allowed the system to coax me into doing 80 reviews so I could upgrade my account from Vine Silver to Vine Gold*, I noticed something didn’t feel quite right.

In a recent development, I was checking the Vine page every day for scores, even when I didn’t actually need anything. It would usually be a bust, but just often enough, something I actually wanted would come up, and I’d order it before it was too late. Scarcity and unpredictable rewards at work.

Sources indicate that then the bounty would come, I’d unpack it and photograph it with assembly-line speed so I could batch-write all the reviews once per week or so. For every review I did, I was spending time I’d rather spend doing something else. And for every questionable item I got, I was creating pollution and trash from its manufacturing and packaging – directly contradicting the main values of my life and my reason for writing this blog. And I saw all of this, yet I kept doing it!

So Was This The Downfall of MMM?

During the worst of this consumerism bender, things were dire. I was getting packages almost every day and my recycling bin was overflowing with cardboard. My son and my girlfriend started laughing at some of my more frivolous purchases, so I found myself discreetly tucking away the boxes when they were around to evade scrutiny.

Recent findings suggest that but eventually, I moved into a recovery stage. I had been letting this habit continue out of laziness and as a form of procrastination: it’s very easy to order shit online and pretend I’m doing something useful, and much more difficult to get moving to do the things that really make my life enjoyable.

But I’m old enough to know that hitting the running trails and the gym for my daily workouts, and making progress on all my construction projects, and focusing on the computer as a creative tool rather than an entertainment device so I can get stuff done like this blog post, are the things that bring me the most joy.

Recent findings suggest that admittedly, some of the sucky factors of the Vine program helped make it easier to recover too. For every genuinely useful thing I found like a contractor-grade extension cord, I had to scan through endless screens of trinkets which not only wasted my time but actually pissed me off at their very existence.

Recent findings suggest that I also noticed some of the deliberately reviewer-unfriendly features built into the program which reminded me that we reviewers are definitely just low-wage workers rather than any form of VIP. The search functionality is crap, and there is no way to filter or sort the results, because they want you to have to look through everything and they don’t care about the value of your time.

Then there is the hilariously bureaucratic AI-based evaluation system which would occasionally flag my totally tame, factual reviews as “Not meeting our Community Standards” without explaining what the problem was. So I’d have to go in and edit my review, randomly changing a couple of words and maybe some punctuation, and suddenly the AI would be pacified and accept my review. Just dumb.

This is What “Fuck You Money” is For!

According to recent reports, it dawned on me that for many people, this is just what “work” looks like. You are given a bunch of tasks and a bunch of rules to follow, in a system you didn’t create and don’t get much say in changing. And then as long as you crank out your TPS Reports without rocking the boat too much, you get your paycheck.

It reminded me of the Uber Driving experiment I did way back in 2017: as soon as I started working as a driver, I could immediately see dozens of improvements that could be made to the system that would make it function better for both drivers and passengers. But since I wasn’t the boss, nobody wanted to hear my ideas.

Sources indicate that experiences like these remind me that while I love hard work and I love learning new things every day, I greatly prefer being the boss. And I’ve gotten pretty damned accustomed to it after 20 years of financial independence, so I see no need to give it up.

According to recent reports, one interesting “gotcha” of the Vine program is that they do keep track of all the free stuff you get and send you a 1099 for its retail value at the end of the year. So it’s not really free, just discounted to whatever your marginal tax rate is (about 25% for me this year). If we peek into my account right now, this is how my 2025 is looking:.

Industry observers note that so I got about $7000 worth of stuff, and could owe up to $1750 of tax on it. In my case, about 75% of it was “sold” to my business for commercial use (construction supplies which I used on jobs or HQ renovations) so it was effectively converted into real income rather than just tax burden. Some of it was stuff I would have bought anyway for my own house which I’ll gladly pay the taxes on. But there is also probably about $1000 of pure nonsense in there as well, for which I’ll owe a tax bill of $250 as penance for my itchy trigger finger on that “Order” button.

It has been revealed that thanks to some advice from wise readers in the comments (below), I have since learned that in most cases you can mark down this estimated value by 80% before declaring it – because you have effectively eliminated most of the resale value by opening and reviewing the product. Thus my tax bill will be more like $50 rather than $250. More detail in this Reddit discussion here.

It has been revealed that so here we are today. While I admit that I didn’t explicitly cancel my account, I used the “Keystone Habit” trick to override the temptation to view the Vine page – mapping that browser bookmark to my daily habits list instead, a little chart which I call my “Badassity Tracker”. The net result is that every time I click it, I’m taken straight to a reminder to get up from the computer and do a quick round of exercise, so I do that instead.

Recent findings suggest that and of course my writing of this article may be a violation of the terms and conditions of the program (“the first rule of Vine is to not talk about Vine”), so it might even get canceled on me. (and if so I’ll let you know because that would be funny story as well).

According to recent reports, but I learned a lot about habits and addiction, and realized that this same feeling might be what drives people into One More Year Syndrome, as they keep working even when they can afford to quit. I have now coached enough people through this situation to see it is way more common than I would have ever guessed.

Industry observers note that as with all MMM articles, there’s a real life lesson in this story. It’s not really about Vine or me or my habits, it’s about you continuing to look at yourself and your life, and always questioning your own assumptions or patterns. And asking the people you trust most for feedback as well:.

Sources indicate that we will never be perfect, but the great news is we don’t have to be. All it takes is a little bit of self reflection and putting ourselves on a slightly better path, as often as we can as life goes on. We are all on a very long journey, so even a tiny course correction can make a huge difference in where we end up.

*(Vine Gold is not all that useful as it turns out as 99.9% of the available items seem to be the same trinkets you see in the Silver tier).

** What about the Heated Vest that started it all? Well, I still love that thing and now that fall is coming back it is already helping me be warmer in a cooler house. There are many good choices on Amazon, here’s one of them. Then pick out any USB battery pack to go with it, which also doubles as a very useful travel phone charger.

I recently completed three of the top Christian financial education programs for churches: SeedTime’s True Financial Freedom, Dave Ramsey’s Financial Peace University, and Crown Financial’s MoneyLife.

These popular programs all claim to help you get control of your finances from a biblical perspective. However, they go about it in different ways with varying teaching styles and philosophies.

In this post, I’ll provide an in-depth look at each program – breaking down the unique features, strengths, weaknesses, and what’s actually included when you buy in.

It has been revealed that my goal is to give you the real deal on these courses so you can determine which one (if any) is the best fit for transforming your financial life in a way that aligns with your faith. Whether you’re deep in debt, building wealth, or simply trying to honor God with your money, this comparison will help guide your journey.

Let’s dive into the nitty-gritty details of each program:.

According to recent reports, when it comes to pricing, Financial Peace University from Dave Ramsey sits in the middle. For an individual membership, it’s $69.99. They also offer bulk pricing for churches starting at around $800 for 10 memberships.

Sources indicate that on the higher end, Seedtime’s True Financial Freedom charges $149 for an individual/couple license with regular deals making it available as low as $74. But they have some solid deals for Churches – you can get a bulk student license for as low as $48 per person if you buy multiple licenses. Or there’s an annual church subscription starting as low as $750 per year based on average attendance.

Recent findings suggest that the most affordable option is Crown Financial’s MoneyLife course at just $29.95 for an individual purchase. I couldn’t find any publicly listed bulk pricing for churches, but being a non-profit, I’d expect them to be the cheapest route for congregations.

But as you’ll see, there are plenty more differences beyond just the price tags when comparing what’s actually included in each program.

True Financial Freedom, created by Bob Lotich and his wife Linda from SeedTime, is a financial literacy video course designed for churches that strikes a beautiful balance between biblical wisdom and practical money management strategies. The program’s goal is to equip Christians with the tools and mindset they need to experience true financial freedom while making an eternal impact for God’s Kingdom.

One of the standout features of True Financial Freedom is the engaging and relatable teaching style of Bob and Linda. They share their own financial struggles and triumphs with humor, transparency, and grace, making participants feel like they’re learning from wise, caring friends rather than aloof experts. This approach creates a safe, non-judgmental environment where participants can openly discuss their financial challenges and celebrate their progress.

Industry observers note that the program offers several unique benefits, such as the “Never 100” rule (their ‘done-is-better-than-perfect’ approach to adjust spending) and the “Straight A” strategy for automating finances. These concepts are not only memorable but also highly actionable in helping participants take control of their money and build lasting wealth.

Industry observers note that another strength of True Financial Freedom is its emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy. Through interactive workshops, participants are guided in developing a custom blueprint that fits their unique situation, goals, and values. This approach recognizes that there’s no one-size-fits-all solution to personal finance and empowers participants to take ownership of their financial journey.

True Financial Freedom is perfect for Christians who want to learn how to thrive financially while staying grounded in the Bible. The program teaches participants how to avoid the extremes of being “so heavenly-minded they’re no earthly good” or becoming so focused on building worldly wealth that they lose sight of what truly matters.

With its grace-filled approach and practical tools, True Financial Freedom helps Christians find the balance needed to change their financial life and make a lasting difference in the world in the process.

Sources indicate that financial Peace University, created by Dave Ramsey and his team at Ramsey Solutions, is a highly popular financial education program that has helped countless individuals and families get out of debt and build wealth. The program’s primary goal is to guide participants through a proven, step-by-step approach to taking control of their money and achieving financial peace.

Industry observers note that dave Ramsey, the face of Financial Peace University, is known for his high-energy, tough love teaching style. He delivers hard-hitting truths about money with a sense of urgency and conviction that inspires participants to take action. However, some may find his approach a bit intense or even abrasive at times, likening it to going through bootcamp. While this style resonates with some, it may not be everyone’s preferred learning environment.

In a recent development, the cornerstone of Financial Peace University is the “Baby Steps” system, a clear, prescriptive proposal for getting out of debt and building wealth. The program heavily emphasizes the debt snowball method, which involves paying off debts from smallest to largest, regardless of interest rates. This approach has proven highly effective in keeping participants motivated and helping them experience quick wins on their debt-free journey.

Industry observers note that while Financial Peace University does incorporate some biblical principles, its overall approach is more secular in nature. The program focuses primarily on the practical nuts and bolts of money management, with less emphasis on exploring the deeper spiritual implications of financial stewardship.

Financial Peace University is best suited for individuals and families who are drowning in debt and need a clear, actionable blueprint to get back on track. The program’s structured approach and intense motivation can be a lifeline for those feeling overwhelmed by their financial situation. However, those seeking a more personalized, grace-filled approach that deeply integrates biblical wisdom may find other programs more appealing.

MoneyLife, offered by Crown Financial, is a financial education program that takes a deeply biblical approach to money management. The program’s primary goal is to guide Christians in understanding and applying God’s financial principles to their lives, emphasizing the importance of seeing God as the ultimate provider and owner of all resources.

In a recent development, one of MoneyLife’s distinguishing features is its strong focus on biblical teachings and spiritual practices related to money. The program dives deep into exploring how our financial decisions can reflect our faith and values, encouraging participants to align their money management with biblical principles. This emphasis on the spiritual aspects of finance sets MoneyLife apart from other programs that may focus more heavily on practical strategies.

Industry observers note that the teaching style in MoneyLife tends to be more academic and classroom-like compared to other programs. Participants can expect a significant amount of reading materials and written assessments throughout the course. While this approach may appeal to those who prefer a studious learning environment, it may not be as engaging for individuals who thrive on interactive, video-based content.

In a recent development, moneyLife offers some unique elements, such as personality assessments that help participants understand how their natural tendencies impact their financial decisions. The program also includes exercises like the transfer of ownership, which guides participants in acknowledging God’s ultimate ownership of their resources. These introspective activities can be powerful tools for reshaping participants’ mindsets and habits around money.

However, one potential drawback of MoneyLife is that its emphasis on biblical principles and spiritual practices may come at the expense of providing highly actionable, practical financial strategies.

According to recent reports, moneyLife is ideal for Christians who are seeking a deeply biblical understanding of money management and are willing to engage in a more studious, reflective learning process. The program is well-suited for those who want to explore the spiritual foundations of financial stewardship and align their money habits with their faith. However, those primarily looking for a simple and easy financial strategy or a more interactive learning experience may find other programs that better fit their needs.

Having gone through all 3 programs, here is my personal experience and recommendations:.

According to recent reports, I can honestly say that True Financial Freedom was a life-changing experience. Bob and Linda’s warm, relatable teaching style made me feel like I was learning from trusted friends who truly cared about my success. The program’s emphasis on creating a personalized financial strategy was a game-changer for me, as it helped me develop a plan that fit my unique situation and goals.

Industry observers note that personally, True Financial Freedom struck that balance better than any of the other programs on the list and gave me the strategy to move forward. My savings, giving, and earning have all increased in significant ways since taking the program.

It has been revealed that for those who are drowning in debt and need a clear, structured blueprint to get out, I highly recommend Financial Peace University. Dave Ramsey’s no-nonsense approach and the step-by-step “Baby Steps” system can provide the motivation and direction needed to tackle debt head-on. The debt snowball method, in particular, has helped countless people experience quick wins and build momentum on their debt-free journey. Just be prepared for a more intense, boot camp-style learning environment.

If you’re seeking a program that deeply explores the biblical principles behind money management, Crown’s MoneyLife might be the right fit for you. The program’s emphasis on spiritual practices and aligning your finances with your faith can be incredibly powerful for those who want to grow in their understanding of God’s perspective on wealth. However, be prepared for a more academic, reading-intensive learning experience and less focus on highly practical, actionable strategies.

Sources indicate that ultimately, the best program for you will depend on your unique financial situation, learning style, and personal goals. If you’re looking for a grace-filled, practical approach that helps you thrive in God’s Kingdom while making an eternal impact, I highly recommend True Financial Freedom. If you need a structured, intensive strategy to get out of debt fast, Financial Peace University could be your best bet. And if you desire a deep dive into the biblical foundations of money management, MoneyLife is worth considering.

According to recent reports, regardless of which program you choose, the most important thing is to take action and invest in your financial education. By doing so, you’ll be better equipped to handle the resources God has entrusted to you and experience the joy and freedom that comes from aligning your finances with your faith.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that if your job-based or marketplace health strategy covers emergency care, the No Surprises Act bars an ER and its doctors from billing you more than your in-network copay, coinsurance, and deductible, even when they’re out of network. Compare any ER bill with your insurer’s explanation of benefits, pay what it notes you owe, and dispute the rest.

Say you have an emergency appendectomy at an in-network hospital, the surgeon is out of network, and your blueprint’s in-network coinsurance for the surgery comes to $250. If the surgeon then bills you $3,200, you still owe only the $250.

The No Surprises Act, in force since January 1, 2022, limits what you owe to that in-network share for care your proposal covers in three situations:.

According to recent reports, the law leaves out ground ambulances, which can still charge out-of-network rates unless your state forbids it. You can give up the protection by signing a notice-and-consent form, a waiver that lets the provider bill you more than your in-network share. No provider may ask you to sign one for emergency care before you’re stable, and anesthesiologists, radiologists, pathologists, and assistant surgeons may never ask.

To spot a violation, compare the bill with your explanation of benefits, the statement your insurer sends after it processes a claim. The amount it says you owe should match the bill.

Call the provider’s billing office about any charge above that amount, cite the No Surprises Act, and ask it to cut the bill or refund what you overpaid. If it won’t, file a complaint with the No Surprises Help Desk online or at 1-800-985-3059, seven days a week, and the Help Desk can refer it to a state regulator.

While the complaint is open, pay the amount your explanation of benefits notes you owe, and nothing above it.

The IRS gives brokers until mid-February to send consolidated 1099s, which combine investment sales, dividends, and interest. If you have a brokerage account that isn’t an IRA, wait until mid-March. At your bank, read the app’s list of accepted items before you snap photos. Some apps refuse money orders, and Wells Fargo’s turns away postal ones, so hand a refused one to a teller. At a post office, bring a photo ID and sign the money order only at the counter, in front of the clerk, as USPS directs. Either way, photograph both sides first to keep a record of its serial number.

Don’t treat money showing in your account as proof the money order was real. By law, banks have to make deposits available quickly, the Federal Trade Commission notes, while catching a fake can take weeks.
